children.title: Support-Function Regularity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Finiteness, continuity, attainment, and information-loss regimes.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and closed convex. Define its recession cone by \(C^\infty:=\{v:x+tv\in C\ \forall x\in C,\ t\ge0\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definition separates three logically distinct questions: whether support is finite, whether a finite supremum is attained, and what set information support data retains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The support-regularity profile of \(C\) is the pair
\[
D_C:=\operatorname{dom}\sigma_C
=\{d:\sigma_C(d)<+\infty\},
\qquad
A_C:=\{d:F_C(d)\neq\varnothing\},
\]
where \(F_C(d)=\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in C}\langle x,d\rangle\). It partitions directions into
\[
A_C\subseteq D_C,
\quad D_C\setminus A_C,
\quad \mathbb{R}^n\setminus D_C,
\]
corresponding respectively to finite attained support, finite unattained support, and infinite support. The finiteness cone is recession-controlled through
\[
\overline{D_C}=(C^\infty)^\circ
:=\{d:\langle v,d\rangle\le0\ \forall v\in C^\infty\}.
\]
The support function is convex and lower semicontinuous everywhere and continuous relative to \(\operatorname{ri}D_C\). Finally, for any nonempty set \(S\),
\[
\sigma_S=\sigma_{\overline{\operatorname{co}}S},
\]
which defines the associated information-loss regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The regularity profile records directions of finite support and directions where that finite value is attained. These distinguish finite attained, finite unattained, and infinite-support regimes. The closure of the finite-support domain is the polar of the recession cone, and the support function is continuous on the relative interior of its domain. Independently, support data loses all distinctions between a set and its closed convex hull.
assumptions_latex: The polar convention is \(K^\circ=\{d:\langle v,d\rangle\le0\ \forall v\in K\}\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(d\in D_C\iff C\) has a finite upper bound in direction \(d\).
\(d\in A_C\iff \exists x\in C\text{ with }\langle x,d\rangle=\sigma_C(d)\).
special_cases_latex: If \(C\) is bounded, then \(D_C=\mathbb{R}^n\).
If \(C\) is compact, then \(A_C=D_C=\mathbb{R}^n\).
If \(C=K\) is a closed convex cone, then \(\sigma_K\) is the indicator of \(K^\circ\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Nonzero recession directions determine where support must become infinite.
Finiteness alone does not guarantee existence of a support point on the boundary of \(D_C\).
boundary_notes: The domain \(D_C\) need not be closed.
The inclusion \(A_C\subseteq D_C\) can be strict even for closed convex sets.
Support functions erase nonconvexity and nonclosedness of the represented set.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite, Lipschitz, and Attained Support for Compact Sets
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(K\subsetaR^n\) be nonempty and compact, and let \(R_K:=\max_{x\in K}\|x\|<+\infty\). Convexity is not required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is the finite-dimensional compact regime. The support function represents the compact convex set \(\operatorname{co}K\), while maximizers may be taken in the original compact set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A nonempty compact set \(K\) is in the compact-set support regime when its support function is everywhere a maximum:
\[
\sigma_K(d)=\max_{x\in K}\langle x,d\rangle\in\mathbb{R}
\quad\forall d\in\mathbb{R}^n.
\]
Its support-point set
\[
F_K(d):=\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in K}\langle x,d\rangle
\]
is nonempty and compact for every \(d\). Moreover,
\[
|\sigma_K(d)|\le R_K\|d\|,
\qquad
|\sigma_K(d_1)-\sigma_K(d_2)|\le R_K\|d_1-d_2\|.
\]
Hence \(\operatorname{dom}\sigma_K=\mathbb{R}^n\), and \(\sigma_K\) is finite, continuous, and globally Lipschitz. It remains closed, convex, and positively homogeneous, and
\[
\sigma_K=\sigma_{\operatorname{co}K}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonempty compact set, every directional support value is finite and attained. The maximizer set is nonempty and compact. The maximal norm of points in the set is a global Lipschitz constant for the support function, so the function is finite and continuous everywhere. The same support function represents the compact convex hull of the set.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\operatorname{dom}\sigma_K=\mathbb{R}^n\) and every direction belongs to the attainment set.
\(\sigma_K|_{\mathbb S^{n-1}}\) is bounded and determines \(\sigma_K\) everywhere by positive homogeneity.
special_cases_latex: If \(K=\{x_0\}\), then \(F_K(d)=\{x_0\}\) for every \(d\).

If \(K\) is compact and strictly convex, then \(F_K(d)\) is a singleton for every \(d
eq0\).
If \(K=rB\), then \(\sigma_K(d)=r\|d\|\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Every nonzero direction defines a supporting hyperplane that meets \(K\).
Uniform convergence of compact-set support functions on the unit ball is the natural metric counterpart of Hausdorff convergence for compact convex sets.
boundary_notes: Compactness, not merely closedness, guarantees attainment in every direction.
The support-point set relative to a nonconvex \(K\) need not be convex, although the exposed face of \(\operatorname{co}K\) is convex.
Differentiability still requires uniqueness of the maximizing point and does not follow from compactness alone.

notation.meaning: maximum Euclidean norm of a point of K

children.title: Recession-Controlled Support Regimes
children.top_down_role: Finite and infinite support directions governed by recession geometry.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Recession-controlled finiteness domain of a support function
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty closed convex set. Its support function is \(\sigma_C(u)=\sup_{x\in C}\langle x,u\rangle\), and its recession cone is \(C_\infty=\{d\in\mathbb{R}^n:x+td\in C\ \forall x\in C,\ \forall t\geq0\}\). For a cone \(K\), use the nonpositive polar \(K^\circ=\{u:\langle d,u\rangle\leq0\ \forall d\in K\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Euclidean regime for nonempty closed convex, possibly unbounded sets; boundary directions of the support-function domain are retained explicitly.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \[\operatorname{dom}\sigma_C:=\{u\in\mathbb{R}^n:\sigma_C(u)<+\infty\},\qquad \overline{\operatorname{dom}\sigma_C}=(C_\infty)^\circ.\] Thus a support direction \(u\) is finite precisely when \(u\in\operatorname{dom}\sigma_C\); every such direction satisfies \(\langle d,u\rangle\leq0\) for all \(d\in C_\infty\), whereas \(u\notin(C_\infty)^\circ\) forces \(\sigma_C(u)=+\infty\). The recession-controlled support regime is the partition of \(\mathbb{R}^n\) into the finite domain \(\operatorname{dom}\sigma_C\), its possibly nonattained boundary inside \((C_\infty)^\circ\), and the infinite-valued complement.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonempty closed convex set \(C\), the finite support directions form \(\operatorname{dom}\sigma_C\), whose closure is the nonpositive polar of the recession cone. Consequently, a direction pairing positively with some recession direction has infinite support value. Recession geometry determines the closure of the finite regime, but it need not determine whether individual boundary directions belong to the domain.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[u\in\operatorname{dom}\sigma_C\iff \exists\beta\in\mathbb{R}\ \text{such that}\ C\subseteq\{x:\langle x,u\rangle\leq\beta\}.\]
\[(C_\infty)^\circ=\overline{\{u:\sup_{x\in C}\langle x,u\rangle<+\infty\}}.\]
special_cases_latex: If \(C\) is bounded, then \(C_\infty=\{0\}\) and \(\operatorname{dom}\sigma_C=\mathbb{R}^n\).
If \(C=K\) is a nonempty closed convex cone, then \(\sigma_K=\iota_{K^\circ}\), so \(\operatorname{dom}\sigma_K=K^\circ\).
immediate_consequences_latex: For every \(u\in\operatorname{dom}\sigma_C\) and \(d\in C_\infty\), one has \(\langle d,u\rangle\leq0\).
The recession cone determines the closure, but not necessarily the exact boundary, of \(\operatorname{dom}\sigma_C\).
boundary_notes: Membership of \(u\in\partial(C_\infty)^\circ\) in \(\operatorname{dom}\sigma_C\) is not guaranteed by recession data alone.
This statement concerns finiteness of the supremum, not attainment by a point of \(C\).

notation.meaning: Recession cone of the closed convex set.
Directions where the support value is finite.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If there exists \(d\in\operatorname{rec}C\) such that \(\langle u,d\rangle>0\), then \[\sigma_C(u)=+\infty.\] The converse fails: for \(C_0=\{(x,t)\in\mathbb{R}^2:t\geq x^2\}\) and \(u_0=(1,0)\), one has \(\sigma_{C_0}(u_0)=+\infty\), although \(\langle u_0,d\rangle=0\) for every \(d\in\operatorname{rec}C_0=\{(0,s):s\geq0\}\).

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\) be a nonempty subset of a real Hilbert space \(H\), and let \(u\in H\setminus\{0\}\). Define \(\sigma_C(u)=\sup_{x\in C}\langle x,u\rangle\) and the exposed support face \(F_C(u)=\{x\in C:\langle x,u\rangle=\sigma_C(u)\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definition applies to noncompact finite-dimensional sets and to infinite-dimensional sets. It separates finiteness of a support value from attainment of the defining supremum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A direction \(u\neq0\) has a support value without a support point when \[\sigma_C(u)<+\infty\quad\text{and}\quad F_C(u)=\varnothing.\] Equivalently, \(C\) is contained in the closed half-space \(\{x:\langle x,u\rangle\leq\sigma_C(u)\}\), this half-space is minimal among those with outward normal \(u\), and its boundary hyperplane \(\{x:\langle x,u\rangle=\sigma_C(u)\}\) does not meet \(C\). Thus the support function records a finite optimal value even though no element of the represented set realizes that value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite support value without a support point occurs when \(\sigma_C(u)\) is finite but no \(x\in C\) satisfies \(\langle x,u\rangle=\sigma_C(u)\). The corresponding limiting supporting hyperplane contains no point of \(C\), despite being the boundary of the smallest closed half-space with normal \(u\) that contains \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[u\text{ is a finite nonattaining support direction}\iff \sigma_C(u)\in\mathbb{R}\ \text{and}\ F_C(u)=\varnothing.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[F_C(u)=\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in C}\langle x,u\rangle,\qquad F_C(u)=\varnothing\ \text{although}\ \sup_{x\in C}\langle x,u\rangle<+\infty.\]
There exists a sequence \((x_k)\subset C\) with \(\langle x_k,u\rangle\to\sigma_C(u)\), but no constant or convergent-to-a-point-of-\(C\) maximizing representative is required.
special_cases_latex: If \(C\) is compact, every continuous linear functional attains its supremum, so this regime is empty.
For \(C=\{(\rho,\tau)\in\mathbb{R}^2:\rho>0,\ \tau\geq1/\rho\}\), finite support values on certain boundary directions of \(\operatorname{dom}\sigma_C\) are not attained.
immediate_consequences_latex: A finite value \(\sigma_C(u)\) alone does not imply \(F_C(u)\neq\varnothing\).
Support-value data cannot by itself certify existence of a maximizing support point.
boundary_notes: The zero direction is excluded because every point trivially realizes \(\sigma_C(0)=0\) when \(C\neq\varnothing\).
Nonattainment may result from nonclosedness, noncompactness, or failure of compactness in the relevant topology; the definition does not prescribe the cause.

children.top_down_role: Set information discarded by support-function representation.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(S,T\) be nonempty subsets of a real Hilbert space \(H\). Their support functions are \(\sigma_S(u)=\sup_{x\in S}\langle x,u\rangle\) and \(\sigma_T(u)=\sup_{x\in T}\langle x,u\rangle\), with values in \(\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert-space support representation of arbitrary nonempty sets; closure and convexification are taken in the norm topology.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define support-equivalence by \[S\sim_\sigma T\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \sigma_S(u)=\sigma_T(u)\ \ \forall u\in H.\] The information discarded by support representation is exactly the distinction among sets having the same closed convex hull: \[\sigma_S=\sigma_{\operatorname{conv}S}=\sigma_{\overline{\operatorname{conv}}S},\qquad S\sim_\sigma T\iff \overline{\operatorname{conv}}S=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}T.\] Hence the canonical set represented by \(\sigma_S\) is \(\overline{\operatorname{conv}}S\), recoverable as the intersection of its support half-spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two nonempty sets are support-equivalent when their support functions agree in every direction. This happens exactly when their closed convex hulls agree. Accordingly, a support function forgets nonconvex arrangement, omitted convex combinations, and nonclosed boundary distinctions, while retaining the unique closed convex hull.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\overline{\operatorname{conv}}S=\bigcap_{u\in H}\{x\in H:\langle x,u\rangle\leq\sigma_S(u)\}.\]
\[\sigma_S=\sigma_T\iff \{x:\langle x,u\rangle\leq\sigma_S(u)\ \forall u\}=\{x:\langle x,u\rangle\leq\sigma_T(u)\ \forall u\}.\]
special_cases_latex: If \(S\) is already closed and convex, then it is uniquely determined by \(\sigma_S\).
A finite set and its polytope hull have identical support functions.
immediate_consequences_latex: Support functions cannot distinguish \(S\) from \(\operatorname{conv}S\), its closure, or any intermediate set with the same closed convex hull.
The support representation becomes injective after restricting its domain to nonempty closed convex sets.
boundary_notes: The statement does not claim that exposed points, extreme points, or topology of the original nonconvex set can be recovered.
The empty set is excluded because conventions for its support function vary.

notation.meaning: Equality of support functions in all directions.
Closed convex hull of the set.

children.top_down_role: Set distinctions erased when support representation passes to closure.

assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a nonempty subset of a finite-dimensional real inner-product space \(X\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(y\in X\),
\[
\sigma_{\operatorname{cl} C}(y)=\sup_{x\in\operatorname{cl} C}\langle x,y\rangle=\sup_{x\in C}\langle x,y\rangle=\sigma_C(y).
\]
Thus the support function cannot distinguish \(C\) from its closure; information carried solely by omitted boundary points is lost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Taking the closure of a nonempty set does not change its support function, so support data cannot detect missing boundary points.
knowledge_statements.title: Closure Information Loss

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Open and Closed Balls Are Support-Indistinguishable
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete finite-dimensional witness that support data do not record boundary inclusion or support attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\neq\{0\}\) be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space, \(B^\circ=\{x:\|x\|<1\}\), and \(B=\{x:\|x\|\leq1\}\). Then \(B^\circ\neq B\), but
\[
\sigma_{B^\circ}(y)=\sigma_B(y)=\|y\|\qquad(y\in X).
\]
For every \(y\neq0\), the supremum is attained on \(B\) but not on \(B^\circ\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The open and closed unit balls have the same support function, although only the closed ball contains maximizing boundary points.
assumptions_latex: \(X\neq\{0\}\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
\(B^\circ\) and \(B\) are its open and closed unit balls.
knowledge_statements.title: Open and Closed Balls Are Support-Indistinguishable

\sigma_{\operatorname{conv} C}(y)=\sup_{x\in\operatorname{conv} C}\langle x,y\rangle=\sup_{x\in C}\langle x,y\rangle=\sigma_C(y).
\]
Consequently, support-function data discard the nonconvex structure of \(C\), retaining only information determined by its convex hull.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The closed convex hull \(D=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv} C)\) is the unique closed convex set having support function \(\sigma_C\). Explicitly,
\[
\sigma_D=\sigma_C,
\qquad
D=\bigcap_{y\in X}\{x\in X:\langle x,y\rangle\leq\sigma_C(y)\}.
\]
The inequalities with \(\sigma_C(y)=+\infty\) impose no restriction. Hence the support function determines exactly the canonical closed-convex representative \(D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set's support function uniquely determines its closed convex hull, represented as the intersection of all support halfspaces.
knowledge_statements.title: Closed-Convex Representative

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The sets \(C\) and \(D\) are support-equivalent precisely when
\[
\sigma_C(y)=\sigma_D(y)\quad\text{for every }y\in X.
\]
In finite dimensions this condition is equivalent to
\[
\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv} C)=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv} D).
\]
Therefore each support-equivalence class consists exactly of all nonempty sets sharing one closed convex hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two nonempty sets have identical support functions exactly when their closed convex hulls coincide.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space and \(C\subseteq H\). The pairing is the inner product \(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle\), and \(\sigma_C(u)=\sup_{x\in C}\langle x,u\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Origin-anchored polarity for arbitrary subsets of a Hilbert space, with the normalization level fixed at one.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The polar set of \(C\) is \[C^\circ:=\{u\in H:\langle x,u\rangle\leq1\ \forall x\in C\}=\{u\in H:\sigma_C(u)\leq1\}.\] The polar is always closed, convex, and contains \(0\). Polarity is order reversing, and the associated bipolar is \[C^{\circ\circ}=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(C\cup\{0\}).\] Consequently, the natural objects fixed by bipolarization are precisely the closed convex subsets containing the origin.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Origin-anchored polarity sends a set \(C\) to all dual vectors whose pairing with every point of \(C\) is at most one. The output is closed, convex, and origin-containing. Applying the operation twice replaces the original set by the closed convex hull of the set together with the origin.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[u\in C^\circ\iff C\subseteq\{x:\langle x,u\rangle\leq1\}.\]
For subsets \(C,D\subseteq H\), \(C\subseteq D^\circ\iff D\subseteq C^\circ\).
special_cases_latex: If \(C\) is a cone, the level-one polar reduces to \(C^\circ=\{u:\langle x,u\rangle\leq0\ \forall x\in C\}\).
If \(C\) is closed, convex, and contains \(0\), then \(C^{\circ\circ}=C\).
immediate_consequences_latex: If \(C\subseteq D\), then \(D^\circ\subseteq C^\circ\).
The polar depends only on \(\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(C\cup\{0\})\).
boundary_notes: The threshold-one polar is origin anchored and is not translation invariant.
The symbol \(C^\circ\) may denote a sign-normalized cone polar in other texts; the normalization is explicit here.

notation.meaning: Bipolar obtained by applying the polar twice.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Threshold, conic, and dual-cone polarity regimes
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(C\subseteq H\), and let \(K\subseteq H\) be a cone. All constructions use the pairing \(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert-space taxonomy distinguishing general origin-anchored set polarity from its homogeneous conic specialization and the opposite-sign dual-cone convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The principal set-polarity regimes are defined by \[C^\odot:=\{u:\sup_{x\in C}\langle x,u\rangle\leq1\},\qquad K^\ominus:=\{u:\sup_{x\in K}\langle x,u\rangle\leq0\},\qquad K^\oplus:=-K^\ominus.\] Here \(C^\odot\) is the threshold-one polar set, \(K^\ominus\) is the nonpositive polar cone, and \(K^\oplus=\{u:\langle x,u\rangle\geq0\ \forall x\in K\}\) is the dual cone. For every cone \(K\), positive homogeneity makes the thresholds one and zero equivalent, so \(K^\odot=K^\ominus\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: General sets use the threshold-one polar. Cones use a homogeneous nonpositive polar because scaling a cone forces every admissible pairing to be nonpositive. The dual cone uses the opposite sign and equals the negative of the polar cone. These conventions coincide only after the sign and conic assumptions are made explicit.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[u\in K^\ominus\iff\langle x,u\rangle\leq0\ \forall x\in K.\]
\[u\in K^\oplus\iff\langle x,u\rangle\geq0\ \forall x\in K.\]
special_cases_latex: For a linear subspace \(V\), \(V^\ominus=V^\oplus=V^\perp\).
For the nonnegative orthant \(K=\mathbb{R}^n_+\), \(K^\oplus=K\) and \(K^\ominus=-K\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Each of \(C^\odot\), \(K^\ominus\), and \(K^\oplus\) is closed and convex; the conic outputs are cones.
Changing between polar-cone and dual-cone conventions changes a sign, not the underlying orthogonality structure.
boundary_notes: The threshold-one construction is not homogeneous for arbitrary sets.
Self-duality refers to \(K=K^\oplus\), not to equality with the nonpositive polar \(K^\ominus\).

children.top_down_role: The standard polarity regime for arbitrary subsets of a dual pair.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-sided unit polar for arbitrary subsets of a separated real dual pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((X,Y,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle)\) be a separated real dual pair and \(C\subseteq X\). Its origin-anchored polar is \[C^\circ=\{y\in Y:\sup_{x\in C}\langle x,y\rangle\le1\}=\{y\in Y:\langle x,y\rangle\le1\ \forall x\in C\}.\] It is \(\sigma(Y,X)\)-closed and convex and contains \(0\). With \(\sup\varnothing=-\infty\), one has \(\varnothing^\circ=Y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The origin-anchored polar consists of dual vectors pairing by at most one with every point of the set; it is weakly closed, convex, and contains zero.
assumptions_latex: \((X,Y,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle)\) is a separated real dual pair.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C^\circ=\{y\in Y:\langle x,y\rangle\le1\ \forall x\in C\}\) is \(\sigma(Y,X)\)-closed, convex, contains \(0\), and \(\varnothing^\circ=Y\).

children.title: Centrally Symmetric Body Polars
children.top_down_role: The balanced convex-body regime underlying norm duality.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
\(B\subseteq X\) is compact, convex, centrally symmetric, and has \(0\in\operatorname{int}B\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B^\circ\) is a centrally symmetric convex body and \(p_{B^\circ}(y)=\sigma_B(y)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Symmetric convex-body polarity and its norm-duality identities.

source_refs.locator: 7.3 Polar Sets p. 136
source_refs.source_title: Convex Analysis and Monotone Operator Theory in Hilbert Spaces

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The polar \(B^\circ\) is again compact, convex, centrally symmetric, and contains \(0\) in its interior. Moreover,
\[
(B^\circ)^\circ=B,
\qquad
p_{B^\circ}(y)=\sigma_B(y),
\qquad
p_B(x)=\sigma_{B^\circ}(x).
\]
Thus \(p_B\) and \(p_{B^\circ}\) are mutually dual norms, with respective closed unit balls \(B\) and \(B^\circ\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polarity sends a centrally symmetric convex body containing the origin internally to another such body and exchanges its gauge with its support function.
knowledge_statements.title: Centrally Symmetric Body Polars

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polar of an origin-symmetric convex body
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(H=\mathbb{R}^n\). Let \(B\subset H\) be a compact convex set with \(0\in\operatorname{int}B\) and \(B=-B\). Define its gauge by \(\gamma_B(x)=\inf\{t>0:x\in tB\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional centrally symmetric convex-body regime underlying norm and dual-norm unit balls.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The polar body of the centrally symmetric convex body \(B\) is \[B^\circ=\{u\in H:\langle x,u\rangle\leq1\ \forall x\in B\}=\{u:\sup_{x\in B}|\langle x,u\rangle|\leq1\}.\] It is again a compact centrally symmetric convex body with \(0\in\operatorname{int}B^\circ\), and \(B^{\circ\circ}=B\). The gauge \(\gamma_B\) is a norm with unit ball \(B\), while \(\gamma_{B^\circ}\) is its dual norm and satisfies \[\gamma_{B^\circ}(u)=\sigma_B(u)=\sup_{\gamma_B(x)\leq1}\langle x,u\rangle.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a compact convex body symmetric about the origin and containing the origin in its interior, the polar consists of vectors pairing with the body by absolute value at most one. The polar is another body of the same type. The gauge of the original body is a norm, and the gauge of the polar is the corresponding dual norm.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[B=\{x:\gamma_B(x)\leq1\},\qquad B^\circ=\{u:\gamma_B^*(u)\leq1\},\] where \(\gamma_B^*=\sigma_B\) denotes the dual norm.
\[\langle x,u\rangle\leq\gamma_B(x)\gamma_{B^\circ}(u)\quad\forall x,u\in H.\]
special_cases_latex: For the Euclidean unit ball \(B_2\), one has \(B_2^\circ=B_2\).
For \(1\leq p\leq\infty\) and Hölder conjugate \(q\), the \(\ell_p\)-unit ball has polar equal to the \(\ell_q\)-unit ball.
immediate_consequences_latex: Central symmetry of \(B\) implies central symmetry of \(B^\circ\).
Boundedness and nonempty interior are exchanged by polarity and, for a convex body containing \(0\) in its interior, both properties hold on each side.
boundary_notes: Without central symmetry, \(\gamma_B\) need not be even and therefore need not be a norm.
If \(0\) is not an interior point, the polar can be unbounded.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Norm–unit-ball correspondence and preservation under polarity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes norms through centrally symmetric closed bounded convex unit balls containing the origin in their interiors and states that polar gauges preserve the norm class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The assignments \(k\mapsto C_k:=\{x:k(x)\leq1\}\) and \(C\mapsto\gamma_C\) define inverse one-to-one correspondences between norms on \(\mathbb{R}^n\) and symmetric closed bounded convex sets \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) satisfying \(0\in\operatorname{int}C\). Moreover, if \(k\) is a norm, then \(k^\circ\) is a norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Norms correspond bijectively to symmetric closed bounded convex unit balls with zero in their interiors: a norm determines its unit ball, and such a set determines its Minkowski gauge. The polar of every norm is again a norm.
assumptions_latex: k\text{ is a norm on }\mathbb{R}^n\text{ when forming }C_k=\{x:k(x)\leq1\}
C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\text{ is symmetric, closed, bounded, and convex with }0\in\operatorname{int}C\text{ when forming }\gamma_C
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: k=\gamma_{C_k},\quad C=\{x:\gamma_C(x)\leq1\},\quad k\leftrightarrow C_k\text{ is a bijection},\qquad k\text{ a norm}\Longrightarrow k^\circ\text{ a norm}.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The polar \(K^\circ\) is a compact convex body with \(0\in\operatorname{int}K^\circ\), and
\[
(K^\circ)^\circ=K,
\qquad
p_K(x)=\sigma_{K^\circ}(x),
\qquad
p_{K^\circ}(y)=\sigma_K(y).
\]
Without central symmetry, \(p_K\) need not satisfy \(p_K(x)=p_K(-x)\); it is a sublinear gauge rather than necessarily a norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonsymmetric convex body containing the origin internally has a polar body; polarity is involutive and exchanges gauges with support functions.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be compact and convex with \(0\in\operatorname{int}C\), without assuming \(C=-C\). Let \(\gamma_C(x)=\inf\{t>0:x\in tC\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex-body polarity beyond balanced or centrally symmetric unit balls.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The polar body is \[C^\circ:=\{u\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle x,u\rangle\leq1\ \forall x\in C\}=\{u:\sigma_C(u)\leq1\}.\] It is a compact convex body containing \(0\) in its interior and satisfies \(C^{\circ\circ}=C\). Its gauge-support correspondence is \[\gamma_C=\sigma_{C^\circ},\qquad \gamma_{C^\circ}=\sigma_C.\] In general \(\gamma_C(x)\neq\gamma_C(-x)\), so the gauge is a positively homogeneous convex asymmetry rather than a norm; polarity nevertheless remains involutive on this class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonsymmetric convex body containing the origin in its interior has the usual threshold-one polar. The polar is again a convex body and the bipolar recovers the original set. The gauges of the two bodies equal the opposite support functions, but the original gauge need not be even and therefore need not define a norm.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[u\in C^\circ\iff\sigma_C(u)\leq1.\]
\[C=\bigcap_{u\in C^\circ}\{x:\langle x,u\rangle\leq1\}.\]
special_cases_latex: If additionally \(C=-C\), the gauge is a norm and this reduces to centrally symmetric norm duality.
For a simplex containing \(0\) in its interior, the polar is a generally nonsymmetric polytope determined by the simplex's facet inequalities.
immediate_consequences_latex: Compactness of \(C\) implies \(0\in\operatorname{int}C^\circ\), while \(0\in\operatorname{int}C\) implies boundedness of \(C^\circ\).
The inequality \(\langle x,u\rangle\leq\gamma_C(x)\gamma_{C^\circ}(u)\) holds without symmetry.
boundary_notes: No absolute value may be inserted into the defining inequality unless the body is centrally symmetric.
If \(0\) lies only on the boundary of \(C\), the polar remains closed and convex but may be unbounded.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sign correspondence between polar and dual cones
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(K\subseteq H\) be a nonempty cone. Define the nonpositive polar and nonnegative dual using the same inner-product pairing.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conic specialization with explicit sign conventions; no closedness or convexity of the input cone is required for the definitions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The polar cone and dual cone of \(K\) are \[K^\ominus:=\{u\in H:\langle x,u\rangle\leq0\ \forall x\in K\},\qquad K^*:=\{u\in H:\langle x,u\rangle\geq0\ \forall x\in K\}.\] They correspond by \[K^*=-K^\ominus.\] Moreover, if \(K\) is viewed as an ordinary set and \(K^\circ=\{u:\langle x,u\rangle\leq1\ \forall x\in K\}\), then conicity gives \(K^\circ=K^\ominus\). Thus the threshold-one set polar specializes exactly to the nonpositive polar cone, while the conventional dual cone differs only by reflection through the origin.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a cone, the nonpositive polar consists of vectors having nonpositive pairing with every cone element, and the dual cone uses nonnegative pairing. The two are negatives of one another. Because cone elements can be scaled arbitrarily, the ordinary threshold-one polar of the underlying set is the same as its nonpositive polar cone.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[u\in K^*\iff -u\in K^\ominus.\]
\[\sup_{x\in K}\langle x,u\rangle\leq1\iff\sup_{x\in K}\langle x,u\rangle\leq0.\]
special_cases_latex: For a subspace \(V\), both signs yield \(V^*=V^\ominus=V^\perp\).
For a self-dual cone, \(K=K^*\) and hence \(K^\ominus=-K\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Both \(K^\ominus\) and \(K^*\) are closed convex cones even when \(K\) is not closed or convex.
If \(K\) is a nonempty closed convex cone, then \(K^{\ominus\ominus}=K\).
boundary_notes: Some authors write \(K^\circ\) for the nonnegative dual rather than the nonpositive polar; formulas must be adjusted by a sign.
The equality between threshold-one and threshold-zero polars relies essentially on conicity.

notation.meaning: Threshold-one polar of the underlying set.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polar cone, dual cone, and self-duality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the nonpositive-pairing convention in a Hilbert space; self-duality is defined only for nonempty convex cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let C\subseteq\mathcal H. The polar cone and dual cone of C are C^{\ominus}=\{u\in\mathcal H\mid \sup_{c\in C}\langle c,u\rangle\leq 0\} and C^{\oplus}=-C^{\ominus}, respectively. If C is a nonempty convex cone, then C is self-dual if C=C^{\oplus}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The polar cone of a subset consists of vectors pairing nonpositively with every point of the subset, and the dual cone is the negative of the polar cone. A nonempty convex cone is self-dual when it equals its dual cone.
assumptions_latex: C\neq\varnothing\text{ and }C\text{ is a convex cone for the self-duality definition}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C^{\ominus}=\{u\in\mathcal H\mid \sup_{c\in C}\langle c,u\rangle\leq 0\},\qquad C^{\oplus}=-C^{\ominus};\qquad C\text{ is self-dual}\iff C=C^{\oplus}\text{ when }C\text{ is a nonempty convex cone}.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The two standard cone conventions differ only by reflection:
\[
K^\ominus=-K^*,
\qquad
K^*=(-K)^\ominus.
\]
Accordingly, any formula written with \(K^\ominus\) and inequalities \(\leq0\) converts to the dual-cone convention by replacing the polar cone with \(-K^*\). The sign convention must therefore be fixed before interpreting cone-polarity identities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Negative polar cones and positive dual cones differ by a minus sign, so formulas must state which convention they use.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Cone polarity reverses inclusion: if \(K_1\subseteq K_2\), then \(K_2^\ominus\subseteq K_1^\ominus\). Its bipolar satisfies
\[
K^{\ominus\ominus}=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}K),
\]
where the right-hand side is the smallest closed convex cone containing \(K\). In particular, polarity is an inclusion-reversing involution on closed convex cones: for such \(K\), \(K^{\ominus\ominus}=K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cone polarity reverses inclusion, and applying it twice returns the closed convex hull of the original cone.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polarity as an antitone Galois transform
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space. For \(C\subseteq H\), define \(C^\circ=\{u:\langle x,u\rangle\leq1\ \forall x\in C\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract set-level calculus generated by the threshold-one polar operation; individual algebraic and transport rules are specializations of this structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The polarity calculus is the antitone correspondence \(\mathcal{P}(H)\to\mathcal{P}(H)\), \(C\mapsto C^\circ\), characterized by \[C\subseteq D^\circ\iff D\subseteq C^\circ.\] It satisfies \[C\subseteq C^{\circ\circ},\qquad C^{\circ\circ\circ}=C^\circ,\qquad C^{\circ\circ}=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(C\cup\{0\}).\] Hence polar calculations may first replace an input by its closed convex origin-containing canonicalization, after which polarity is an order-reversing involution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Set polarity is an antitone Galois correspondence: one set lies in the polar of another exactly when the reverse inclusion holds after exchanging the sets. Every set lies in its bipolar, triple polarity equals single polarity, and bipolarization is closed convex origin-containing canonicalization.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[C\subseteq D\Longrightarrow D^\circ\subseteq C^\circ.\]

The map \(C\mapsto C^{\circ\circ}\) is extensive, monotone, and idempotent: \(C\subseteq C^{\circ\circ}\), \(C\subseteq D\Rightarrow C^{\circ\circ}\subseteq D^{\circ\circ}\), and \(C^{\circ\circ\circ\circ}=C^{\circ\circ}\).
special_cases_latex: On closed convex sets containing \(0\), polarity is an antitone involution.
On cones, the same calculus uses the homogeneous nonpositive polar.
immediate_consequences_latex: Any identity between canonical closed convex origin-containing sets can be dualized by reversing inclusions and applying the polar.
The polar of an arbitrary set is unchanged by closure, convexification, or adjoining the origin.
boundary_notes: The transform is not a Boolean complement and does not exchange arbitrary intersections and unions without convex closure operations.
Translations are not intrinsic operations of origin-anchored polarity.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closed-convex origin hull as polar-invariant canonicalization
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space and \(C\subseteq H\). Define \(C^\circ=\{u:\langle x,u\rangle\leq1\ \forall x\in C\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Norm-closed Hilbert-space canonicalization associated with threshold-one set polarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The polar-invariant canonicalization of \(C\) is \[\operatorname{can}_\circ(C):=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(C\cup\{0\})=C^{\circ\circ}.\] It is the smallest closed convex set containing both \(C\) and the origin, and it is polar invariant in the sense that \[\operatorname{can}_\circ(C)^\circ=C^\circ.\] Two sets therefore have the same polar exactly when their polar canonicalizations coincide: \[C^\circ=D^\circ\iff\operatorname{can}_\circ(C)=\operatorname{can}_\circ(D).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: To canonicalize a set without changing its polar, adjoin the origin, take the convex hull, and close it. This set equals the bipolar and is the smallest closed convex origin-containing superset. Equality of polars is equivalent to equality of these canonicalized sets.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[C^\circ=(C\cup\{0\})^\circ=(\operatorname{conv}(C\cup\{0\}))^\circ=(\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(C\cup\{0\}))^\circ.\]
\[C^\circ=D^\circ\iff C^{\circ\circ}=D^{\circ\circ}.\]
special_cases_latex: If \(0\in C\), then \(\operatorname{can}_\circ(C)=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}C\).
If \(C\) is closed, convex, and contains \(0\), then \(\operatorname{can}_\circ(C)=C\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Canonicalization is idempotent: \(\operatorname{can}_\circ(\operatorname{can}_\circ(C))=\operatorname{can}_\circ(C)\).
Any polar formula may replace each input set by its canonicalization without changing the result.
boundary_notes: Ordinary closed convex hull without adjoining \(0\) is insufficient when \(0\notin\overline{\operatorname{conv}}C\).
Closure is taken in the ambient Hilbert-space norm topology.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Union, intersection, and scaling rules for polar sets
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \((C_i)_{i\in I}\) be subsets of a real Hilbert space \(H\), and define \(C^\circ=\{u:\langle x,u\rangle\leq1\ \forall x\in C\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic set-algebra rules for threshold-one polarity; intersection formulas require closed convex origin-containing inputs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Set-algebra polarity is governed by \[\left(\bigcup_{i\in I}C_i\right)^\circ=\bigcap_{i\in I}C_i^\circ,\qquad (\lambda C)^\circ=\lambda^{-1}C^\circ\quad(\lambda>0).\] Since a polar is insensitive to closed convex origin-containing hulls, also \[\left(\overline{\operatorname{conv}}\left(\bigcup_{i\in I}C_i\cup\{0\}\right)\right)^\circ=\bigcap_{i\in I}C_i^\circ.\] For two closed convex sets \(C,D\) containing \(0\), the dual intersection rule is \[(C\cap D)^\circ=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(C^\circ\cup D^\circ).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The polar of a union is the intersection of the individual polars, positive scaling is inverted, and convexifying or closing a union does not change its polar. Conversely, for closed convex origin-containing sets, the polar of an intersection is the closed convex hull of the union of their polars.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[u\in\left(\bigcup_iC_i\right)^\circ\iff u\in C_i^\circ\ \forall i.\]
For closed convex \(C,D\ni0\), \(C\cap D=(\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(C^\circ\cup D^\circ))^\circ\).
special_cases_latex: For cones under the nonpositive convention, \((K_1+K_2)^\circ=K_1^\circ\cap K_2^\circ\).
For a finite family of closed convex origin-containing sets, the intersection rule iterates with a final closed convex hull.
immediate_consequences_latex: Polarity reverses inclusion and converts generated hulls into intersections.
The closure in the intersection rule cannot generally be omitted in infinite-dimensional spaces.
boundary_notes: There is no unconditional formula \((C\cap D)^\circ=C^\circ\cup D^\circ\); convexification and usually closure are essential.
The scaling rule stated here assumes \(\lambda>0\); negative scaling introduces reflection.

notation.meaning: Set obtained by scaling the polar by the reciprocal positive scalar.

children.title: Closure-Sensitive Set Algebra
children.top_down_role: Closure plus convexification effects in polarity identities for combined sets.

assumptions_latex: \((C_i)_{i\in I}\) is a nonempty family of subsets of \(H\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\bigcup_i C_i)^\circ=\bigcap_i C_i^\circ\), while intersection polarity generally requires closed convexification.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes exact union laws from closure-sensitive intersection laws.

source_refs.locator: 7.3 Polar Sets p. 136

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Polarity converts arbitrary unions exactly into intersections: \[\left(\bigcup_{i\in I}C_i\right)^\circ=\bigcap_{i\in I}C_i^\circ.\] By contrast, if every \(C_i\) is closed, convex, and contains \(0\), then \[\left(\bigcap_{i\in I}C_i\right)^\circ=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}\left(\bigcup_{i\in I}C_i^\circ\right),\] and omission of the closure can fail in infinite-dimensional spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Union polarity is exact, whereas intersection polarity generally needs both convexification and closure.
knowledge_statements.title: Closure-Sensitive Set Algebra

source_witnesses.locator: 7.3 Polar Sets p. 136

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Infinite-dimensional subspace example showing that closed convexification cannot generally be replaced by algebraic convexification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E=\ell^2\), let \(T:E\to E\) be \(T(x_n)=(x_n/n)\), and in \(H=E\oplus E\) set \[M=E\oplus\{0\},\qquad N=\operatorname{gra}T.\] Then \(M,N\) are closed subspaces but \(M+N=E\oplus\operatorname{ran}T\) is not closed. With \(C_1=M^\perp\) and \(C_2=N^\perp\), \[C_1^\circ=M,\qquad C_2^\circ=N,\] and \[(C_1\cap C_2)^\circ=\overline{M+N}\supsetneq M+N=\operatorname{conv}(C_1^\circ\cup C_2^\circ).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two closed subspaces with a nonclosed sum yield closed convex origin-containing sets for which intersection polarity strictly requires closure.
knowledge_statements.title: Indispensable Closure in Intersection Polarity

children.title: Linear-Adjoint Polarity Transport
children.top_down_role: Polarity under linear transformations and adjoints.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polar transport through a linear map and its adjoint
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X=\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(Y=\mathbb{R}^m\) be Euclidean spaces, let \(A:X\to Y\) be linear, and let \(A^*:Y\to X\) satisfy \(\langle Ax,y\rangle_Y=\langle x,A^*y\rangle_X\). Let \(C\subseteq X\) be nonempty.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional linear-image transport for threshold-one polar sets; the image need not be closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Linear-adjoint polarity transport is the identity \[(A C)^\circ=(A^*)^{-1}(C^\circ)=\{y\in Y:A^*y\in C^\circ\}.\] Equivalently, support functions transform by \[\sigma_{A C}(y)=\sigma_C(A^*y)\quad\forall y\in Y.\] Since support functions and polars are unchanged by closure, the same formulas hold with \(AC\) replaced by \(\overline{AC}\). Thus a primal linear image is tested in the dual space by pulling the test vector back through the adjoint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The polar of a linear image consists exactly of dual vectors whose adjoint pullback lies in the original polar. Equivalently, the support function of the image at \(y\) equals the support function of the original set at \(A^*y\). Closing the image does not alter either identity.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[y\in(AC)^\circ\iff\langle Ax,y\rangle\leq1\ \forall x\in C\iff A^*y\in C^\circ.\]
\[(\overline{AC})^\circ=(AC)^\circ.\]
special_cases_latex: If \(A\) is orthogonal, then \((AC)^\circ=A(C^\circ)\).
If \(A\) is invertible, then \((AC)^\circ=A^{-*}C^\circ\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The kernel of \(A^*\) is always contained in \((AC)^\circ\).
Linear image support calculations can be performed without explicitly constructing \(AC\).
boundary_notes: A formula for the polar of an inverse image generally involves image closure and additional structure; it is not asserted here.
Closedness of \(AC\) is not automatic, even when \(C\) is closed and convex.

notation.meaning: Inverse of the adjoint when \(A\) is invertible.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The kernel and range satisfy \[(\ker T)^\circ=(\ker T)^\perp=\overline{\operatorname{ran}T^*},\qquad (\operatorname{ran}T)^\circ=(\operatorname{ran}T)^\perp=\ker T^*.\] The equality \((\ker T)^\circ=\operatorname{ran}T^*\) holds exactly when \(\operatorname{ran}T^*\) is closed, equivalently when \(\operatorname{ran}T\) is closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The polar of the kernel is the closed adjoint range, while the polar of the range is the adjoint kernel; the closure on the adjoint range can be dropped exactly under the closed-range condition.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A compact diagonal injection has a proper dense adjoint range, so the closure in the kernel-polar formula is essential.

knowledge_statements.title: Dense Nonclosed Adjoint Range

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp density consequences of the kernel and range polar identities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a bounded linear operator \(T:X\to Y\) between real Hilbert spaces, \[\ker T=\{0\}\iff \overline{\operatorname{ran}T^*}=X,\qquad \overline{\operatorname{ran}T}=Y\iff \ker T^*=\{0\}.\] Thus injectivity corresponds to density, not necessarily surjectivity, of the adjoint range.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Injectivity is dual to density of the adjoint range, and dense range is dual to injectivity of the adjoint.
knowledge_statements.title: Injectivity and Dense-Range Polar Boundaries

children.title: Product-Space Polarity Calculus
children.top_down_role: Polarity in product-space and marginal constructions.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polar and marginal rules in a product space
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X=\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(Y=\mathbb{R}^m\), paired componentwise by \(\langle(x,y),(u,v)\rangle=\langle x,u\rangle+\langle y,v\rangle\). Let \(C\subseteq X\), \(D\subseteq Y\), and \(S\subseteq X\times Y\) be nonempty.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional threshold-one polarity for Cartesian products and coordinate projections.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Cartesian-product support function separates as \[\sigma_{C\times D}(u,v)=\sigma_C(u)+\sigma_D(v),\] and hence \[(C\times D)^\circ=\{(u,v):\sigma_C(u)+\sigma_D(v)\leq1\}.\] If \(P_X(x,y)=x\) is the coordinate projection, then the polar of the marginal projection is the zero-slice of the product-space polar: \[(P_XS)^\circ=\{u\in X:(u,0)\in S^\circ\}.\] Thus products produce additive support constraints, while projection in the primal space becomes restriction to a coordinate slice in the polar space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a product space, the support value of a Cartesian product is the sum of the two component support values. Its polar is therefore a coupled sublevel set, not generally the product of the component polars. Projecting a set onto one coordinate corresponds to intersecting its polar with the complementary dual coordinate set to zero.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[(u,v)\in(C\times D)^\circ\iff \sup_{x\in C}\langle x,u\rangle+\sup_{y\in D}\langle y,v\rangle\leq1.\]
\[u\in(P_XS)^\circ\iff\langle x,u\rangle\leq1\ \forall(x,y)\in S.\]
special_cases_latex: For nonempty cones \(K,L\), \((K\times L)^\ominus=K^\ominus\times L^\ominus\), because each support term must be nonpositive.
If \(D=\{0\}\), then \((C\times\{0\})^\circ=C^\circ\times Y\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The general identity \((C\times D)^\circ=C^\circ\times D^\circ\) is false for threshold-one polarity.
Marginal polar constraints can be read directly from the zero-coordinate slice of \(S^\circ\).
boundary_notes: The additive formula uses the componentwise product pairing.
For infinite products, topological-dual and summability choices require separate specification.

notation.meaning: Threshold-one polar in the product pairing.

children.title: Slice Polarity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit finite-dimensional example showing that closure in central-slice polarity is indispensable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[K=\{(a,b,c)\in\mathbb R^2\times\mathbb R:a\ge0,\ c\ge0,\ 2ac\ge b^2\}\] and let \(C=K^\ominus\), where \(K^\ominus=\{z:\langle z,k\rangle\le0\ \forall k\in K\}\). Then \(C^\circ=K\), while \[\pi_{\mathbb R^2}(K)=\{(a,b):a>0\}\cup\{(0,0)\}\] is not closed. Hence, for \(S=\{x:(x,0)\in C\}\), \[S^\circ=\overline{\pi_{\mathbb R^2}(C^\circ)}\supsetneq\pi_{\mathbb R^2}(C^\circ).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rotated second-order cone has a nonclosed coordinate projection, producing a central slice whose polar strictly exceeds the unclosed projection of the original polar.
assumptions_latex: The spaces are finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces.
\(K\) and \(C\) are the displayed closed convex cones.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonclosed Polar Projection Counterexample

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sufficient exactness regime for central-slice polarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(0\in\operatorname{int}C\), then \(C^\circ\) is compact and therefore \(\pi_X(C^\circ)\) is closed. Consequently, for \(S=\{x:(x,0)\in C\}\), \[S^\circ=\pi_X(C^\circ).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the origin is interior to the product-space set, its polar is compact and the closure in the central-slice formula may be omitted.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq X\times Y\) is closed and convex.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polar representation for a noncentral coordinate fiber under a relative-interior qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[S_{y_0}=\{x\in X:(x,y_0)\in C\}.\] If \(y_0\in\operatorname{ri}(\pi_YC)\), then \[S_{y_0}^\circ=\left\{u\in X:\exists v\in Y,\ \sigma_C(u,v)-\langle v,y_0\rangle\le1\right\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the relative-interior qualification, the polar of an affine coordinate slice is a projection of a support-function sublevel set incorporating the slice offset.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq X\times Y\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.

assumptions_latex: C\subseteq X\times Y\text{ is closed and convex}

notation.meaning: central slice of C, identified with a subset of X

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Central slices of closed convex sets in finite-dimensional product spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C^\circ=\{(u,v)\in X\times Y:\langle u,x\rangle+\langle v,y\rangle\le 1\text{ for every }(x,y)\in C\}\), and let \(S=\{x\in X:(x,0)\in C\}\). Then the polar of the central slice is the closure of the coordinate projection of the product-space polar:
\[
S^\circ=\operatorname{cl}\!\left(\pi_X(C^\circ)\right).
\]
The closure cannot in general be omitted because a linear image of a closed convex set need not be closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The polar of a central slice equals the closure of the corresponding coordinate projection of the original set’s polar.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(C^\circ=\{(u,v):\langle u,x\rangle+\langle v,y\rangle\le1\text{ for every }(x,y)\in C\}\). A vector \(u\in X\) belongs to the polar of \(\pi_XC\) exactly when its zero extension \((u,0)\) belongs to \(C^\circ\). Thus
\[
(\pi_X C)^\circ=\{u\in X:(u,0)\in C^\circ\}.
\]
No convexity or closedness assumption on \(C\) is required.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Paired projection and central-slice identities for Euclidean product spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
With the unit-polar convention, coordinate projection and zero-coordinate slicing exchange roles under polarity. Explicitly,
\[
(\pi_XC)^\circ=\iota_X^{-1}(C^\circ),
\qquad
\{x:(x,0)\in C\}^\circ_X=\operatorname{cl}(\pi_XC^\circ).
\]
The first identity holds for arbitrary \(C\subseteq X\times Y\); the stated closedness, convexity, and origin assumptions ensure the second identity. The analogous pair follows after interchanging \(X\) and \(Y\).

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(C\subseteq H\). Define \(C^\circ=\{u\in H:\langle x,u\rangle\leq1\ \forall x\in C\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert-space threshold-one bipolar family, including the fixed-point representation class and its conic specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The bipolar operator is \[\mathfrak{b}(C):=C^{\circ\circ}=\{x\in H:\langle x,u\rangle\leq1\ \forall u\in C^\circ\}.\] Its canonical value is \[\mathfrak{b}(C)=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(C\cup\{0\}).\] Therefore \(C\) admits exact polar representation, meaning \(C=C^{\circ\circ}\), precisely when \(C\) is closed, convex, and contains \(0\). For a cone \(K\), threshold-one polarity becomes homogeneous nonpositive polarity and \(K^{\circ\circ}=\overline{\operatorname{cone}}K\); hence a cone is bipolar exactly when it is closed and convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The bipolar of a set consists of all points satisfying every unit-threshold inequality indexed by the polar. It equals the closed convex hull after adjoining the origin. The fixed points are exactly closed convex origin-containing sets. In the conic regime, the bipolar is the closed convex conical hull.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[C^{\circ\circ}=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(C\cup\{0\}),\qquad C=C^{\circ\circ}\iff C\text{ is closed, convex, and }0\in C.\]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polar Cone and Conic Bipolar Closure
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space with inner product \(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle\), and let \(S\subseteq H\) be nonempty. Write \(\operatorname{cone}S\) for its conic hull and \(\overline{\operatorname{cone}}S\) for the norm closure of that hull.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert-space negative-polar convention; the finite-dimensional Euclidean statement is obtained by taking \(H=\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \[S^{\ominus}:=\{u\in H:\sup_{x\in S}\langle x,u\rangle\le 0\}=\{u\in H:(\forall x\in S)\ \langle x,u\rangle\le0\}.\] The conic bipolar of \(S\) is \(S^{\ominus\ominus}:=(S^{\ominus})^{\ominus}\), and conic bipolarity is the identity \[S^{\ominus\ominus}=\overline{\operatorname{cone}}S.\] Consequently, a nonempty cone \(K\) satisfies \(K^{\ominus\ominus}=K\) exactly when it is closed and convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The polar cone of a nonempty set \(S\) consists of all vectors making a nonpositive inner product with every point of \(S\). Applying this operation twice produces the closed convex cone generated by \(S\). Thus repeated conic polarity is a closure-and-convexification operation, and it fixes precisely the nonempty closed convex cones.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[S^{\ominus\ominus}=\overline{\operatorname{cone}}S,\qquad K^{\ominus\ominus}=K\ \Longleftrightarrow\ K\text{ is a nonempty closed convex cone}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: With the dual-cone convention \(S^{\oplus}:=-S^{\ominus}\), one has \(S^{\oplus\oplus}=\overline{\operatorname{cone}}S\).
For \(x\in H\), \(x\in\overline{\operatorname{cone}}S\) if and only if every \(u\in H\) satisfying \(\langle s,u\rangle\le0\) for all \(s\in S\) also satisfies \(\langle x,u\rangle\le0\).
special_cases_latex: If \(K\subseteq H\) is already a nonempty closed convex cone, then \(K^{\ominus\ominus}=K\).
If \(V\subseteq H\) is a closed linear subspace, then \(V^{\ominus}=V^\perp\) and \(V^{\ominus\ominus}=V\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The polar is invariant under conic convex closure: \(S^{\ominus}=(\overline{\operatorname{cone}}S)^{\ominus}\).
Polarity reverses inclusion: \(S_1\subseteq S_2\Rightarrow S_2^{\ominus}\subseteq S_1^{\ominus}\).
boundary_notes: Without closedness or convexity, a cone need not equal its bipolar; the bipolar supplies both missing regularizations.
The sign convention differs from the nonnegative dual cone used in some conic-optimization texts.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Work in \(\mathbb R^n\) with its Euclidean pairing. Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a closed convex set containing \(0\), and define \(C^\circ:=\{y:\langle x,y\rangle\le1\text{ for every }x\in C\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional closed convex sets anchored at the origin; the representation uses normalized supporting halfspaces whose offsets equal one.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The polar representation family of \(C\) is \[\mathcal H(C):=\{H_y:y\in C^\circ\},\qquad H_y:=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\langle x,y\rangle\le1\}.\] Its represented set is \[R(C):=\bigcap_{y\in C^\circ}H_y=C^{\circ\circ}.\] Since \(C\) is closed, convex, and contains \(0\), bipolarity gives \[C=R(C)=\bigcap_{y\in C^\circ}\{x:\langle x,y\rangle\le1\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed convex set containing the origin is represented by all normalized closed halfspaces indexed by its polar. A point belongs to the set exactly when it satisfies every inequality \(\langle x,y\rangle\le1\) with \(y\in C^\circ\). The intersection of these halfspaces is the bipolar and hence recovers \(C\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: The representation may be written as the support-function test \(x\in C\Longleftrightarrow\sigma_{C^\circ}(x)\le1\).
Equivalently, \(C\) is the unit sublevel set of the support function of its polar: \(C=\{x:\sigma_{C^\circ}(x)\le1\}\).
special_cases_latex: For a closed convex cone \(K\), normalization collapses to homogeneous inequalities and \(K=K^{\ominus\ominus}\).
If \(C\) is bounded with \(0\in\operatorname{int}C\), then \(C^\circ\) is also a convex body containing \(0\) in its interior.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every point outside \(C\) violates at least one polar inequality: \(x\notin C\Rightarrow(\exists y\in C^\circ)\ \langle x,y\rangle>1\).
The gauge-support identity is \(\gamma_C=\sigma_{C^\circ}\).
boundary_notes: If \(C\) is not closed, convex, or origin-containing, the same intersection represents \(\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(C\cup\{0\})\), not necessarily \(C\).
Not every indexed halfspace must define a facet or an irredundant constraint.

children.title: Bipolar Regularity Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Boundaries caused by missing convexity, closure, origin inclusion, or the appropriate dual topology.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bipolar Regularization and Its Fixed Points
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be arbitrary and define \(C^\circ:=\{y\in\mathbb R^n:(\forall x\in C)\ \langle x,y\rangle\le1\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Euclidean polarity; this entry isolates exactly which regularity properties are imposed by taking the bipolar.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The bipolar regularization of \(C\) is \[\mathcal B(C):=C^{\circ\circ}.\] It has the explicit form \[\mathcal B(C)=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(C\cup\{0\}).\] Accordingly, \(C\) is a fixed point of bipolar regularization, meaning \(\mathcal B(C)=C\), if and only if \(C\) is closed, convex, and contains the origin.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The bipolar of an arbitrary finite-dimensional set is its closed convex hull after adjoining the origin. This formula records the three regularity boundaries of ordinary set polarity: convexification repairs missing convexity, closure repairs missing closedness, and adjoining zero repairs failure of origin inclusion. Equality with the original set occurs exactly when none of those repairs changes it.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[C^{\circ\circ}=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(C\cup\{0\}),\qquad C^{\circ\circ}=C\Longleftrightarrow C\text{ is closed, convex, and }0\in C.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(C^\circ\) depends only on the regularization: \(C^\circ=\mathcal B(C)^\circ\).
\(\mathcal B\) is an extensive, monotone, idempotent closure operator on subsets of \(\mathbb R^n\).
special_cases_latex: If \(C\) is convex and contains \(0\) but is not closed, then \(C^{\circ\circ}=\operatorname{cl}C\).
If \(C\) is closed and convex but \(0\notin C\), then \(C^{\circ\circ}=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(C\cup\{0\})\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Different sets with the same closed origin-containing convex hull have the same polar.
The polar \(C^\circ\) is always closed, convex, and origin-containing, regardless of the regularity of \(C\).
boundary_notes: In an infinite-dimensional dual pair, closure must be taken in the topology determined by the chosen duality, commonly the appropriate weak topology.
For conic polarity with threshold zero, the corresponding regularization is the closed convex conic hull.

children.title: Bipolar Closure Regimes
children.top_down_role: Closure operations relevant to recovery from repeated polarity.

assumptions_latex: (X,Y)\text{ is a separating real dual pair}

notation.meaning: convex hull after adjoining the origin

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact effects of bipolarization under progressively stronger regularity assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(B=\operatorname{conv}(A\cup\{0\})\). Bipolarization always yields
\[
A^{\circ\circ}=\overline{B}^{\,\sigma(X,Y)}.
\]
Hence, if \(A\) is convex and contains \(0\), then \(A^{\circ\circ}=\overline{A}^{\,\sigma(X,Y)}\). If \(A\) is additionally \(\sigma(X,Y)\)-closed, then \(A^{\circ\circ}=A\). These are the convexification, origin-adjunction, and closure regimes of the same operation, not distinct bipolar conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bipolarization successively accounts for the missing origin, missing convexity, and missing weak closedness; exact recovery occurs when all three already hold.
knowledge_statements.title: Bipolar Closure Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record correctly distinguishes origin adjunction, convexification, weak closure, and exact recovery, and property is suitable for the Bipolar Closure Regimes container. It has no authoritative source or specific locator.

children.title: Dual-Topology Selection
children.top_down_role: Topological choices determined by the available dual pairing.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Incompatible Topologies Can Change Convex Closure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An infinite-dimensional failure of replacing dual-pair weak closure by closure in a topology having a smaller continuous dual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X=\ell^1\), pair it with \(Y=\ell^\infty\), and let \(\tau=\sigma(\ell^1,c_0)\). Define
\[
C=\left\{x\in\ell^1:\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}x_n=0\right\}.
\]
The functional \(\mathbf 1=(1,1,\ldots)\) belongs to \(Y\setminus c_0\). The subspace \(C=\ker\mathbf1\) is \(\sigma(\ell^1,\ell^\infty)\)-closed, whereas it is \(\tau\)-dense in \(\ell^1\). Consequently,
\[
\overline C^{\,\sigma(\ell^1,\ell^\infty)}=C,
\qquad
\overline C^{\,\tau}=\ell^1.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On l1, the kernel of the summation functional is closed for the weak topology induced by l-infinity but dense for the weaker topology induced by c0, so convex closures need not agree without dual compatibility.

notation.meaning: weak topology induced on E by the separating space F
space of scalar sequences converging to zero

knowledge_statements.title: Incompatible Topologies Can Change Convex Closure

assumptions_latex: (X,Y)\text{ is a separating real dual pair}
\tau\text{ is a locally convex topology on }X

notation.meaning: continuous dual of the locally convex space

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Topology compatibility required to replace weak closure by another locally convex closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A locally convex topology \(\tau\) is compatible with the dual pair when its continuous dual is exactly \(Y\), namely \((X,\tau)'=Y\). Under this condition, every convex subset of \(X\) has the same \(\tau\)-closure as its \(\sigma(X,Y)\)-closure. Therefore, for every \(A\subseteq X\),
\[
A^{\circ\circ}=\overline{\operatorname{conv}(A\cup\{0\})}^{\,\tau}=\overline{\operatorname{conv}(A\cup\{0\})}^{\,\sigma(X,Y)}.
\]
Without compatibility, substituting \(\tau\)-closure is not generally valid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any compatible locally convex topology gives the same closure of convex sets as the weak topology, so either closure computes the bipolar.
knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Topology Selection

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The compatibility condition and equality of closures for convex sets are stated with the necessary locally convex and continuous-dual hypotheses. Condition is the correct content kind for Dual-Topology Selection, but the claim requires an authoritative source with a specific locator.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), where \(\mathbb R^n\) is identified with its dual by the Euclidean inner product.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical finite-dimensional, one-sided polarity with normalization level one; no convexity or closedness is needed to form the polar.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Euclidean polar of \(C\) is \[C^\circ:=\{y\in\mathbb R^n:\langle x,y\rangle\le1\ \text{for every }x\in C\}=\{y:\sigma_C(y)\le1\}.\] The operation is inclusion reversing: \[C_1\subseteq C_2\Longrightarrow C_2^\circ\subseteq C_1^\circ.\] Every polar is a closed convex set containing \(0\), and repeated polarity satisfies \[C^{\circ\circ}=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(C\cup\{0\}).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The polar of a set in Euclidean space is the collection of vectors whose inner product with every point of the set is at most one. It is equivalently the unit sublevel set of the support function. Polarity reverses containment, always produces a closed convex origin-containing set, and its second application produces the closed convex hull of the original set together with the origin.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(y\in C^\circ\Longleftrightarrow\sup_{x\in C}\langle x,y\rangle\le1\).
For closed convex \(C\) containing \(0\), \(x\in C\Longleftrightarrow\langle x,y\rangle\le1\) for every \(y\in C^\circ\).
special_cases_latex: \(\{0\}^\circ=\mathbb R^n\) and \((\mathbb R^n)^\circ=\{0\}\).
For the Euclidean unit ball \(B_2\), \(B_2^\circ=B_2\).
immediate_consequences_latex: \((\lambda C)^\circ=\lambda^{-1}C^\circ\) for every \(\lambda>0\).
If \(C\) is closed and convex with \(0\in C\), then \(C\mapsto C^\circ\) is an involution on that class.
boundary_notes: This polar is generally not centrally symmetric; symmetry of \(C^\circ\) requires corresponding symmetry of \(C\).
For cones, the level-one definition reduces to the homogeneous nonpositive polar-cone inequality.

children.title: Polar-Polytope Face Duality
children.top_down_role: Combinatorial duality between the facial structures of polar polytopes.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(P\subset\mathbb R^d\) be a full-dimensional polytope with \(0\in\operatorname{int}P\), and let \(Q=P^\circ\). Include \(\varnothing\) and the whole polytope among the faces.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Full-dimensional finite polytopes whose polar is taken about an interior origin.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every face \(F\) of \(P\), define its polar-dual face by \[F^\diamond:=\{y\in Q:\langle x,y\rangle=1\ \text{for every }x\in F\},\] with \(\varnothing^\diamond=Q\) and \(P^\diamond=\varnothing\). Then \(F^\diamond\) is a face of \(Q\), the map \(F\mapsto F^\diamond\) is a bijection between the face lattices of \(P\) and \(Q\), and it reverses inclusion. For every proper nonempty face, \[\dim F+\dim F^\diamond=d-1.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A face of a polytope containing the origin in its interior determines the face of the polar on which all points of the original face pair to one. This assignment is an inclusion-reversing bijection of face lattices. It interchanges the empty and whole faces and sends a \(k\)-dimensional proper face to a \((d-1-k)\)-dimensional face.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For a face \(G\) of \(Q\), its inverse image is \(G^\diamond=\{x\in P:\langle x,y\rangle=1\text{ for every }y\in G\}\).
The face lattices \(\mathcal F(P)\) and \(\mathcal F(P^\circ)\) are anti-isomorphic.
special_cases_latex: Vertices of \(P\) correspond to facets of \(P^\circ\), and facets of \(P\) correspond to vertices of \(P^\circ\).
In dimension three, edges correspond to edges, while vertices and facets are interchanged.
immediate_consequences_latex: The face numbers satisfy \(f_k(P)=f_{d-1-k}(P^\circ)\).
Combinatorial simplicity of \(P\) corresponds to simpliciality of \(P^\circ\).
boundary_notes: The hypothesis \(0\in\operatorname{int}P\) ensures that \(P^\circ\) is a full-dimensional polytope and that the level-one face correspondence is well defined.
For lower-dimensional or unbounded polyhedra, the stated face-lattice duality requires modification.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Inclusion-Reversing Face Duality of Polar Polytopes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Face-lattice correspondence between a polytope containing the origin in its interior and its polar, including improper-face conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) be a polytope with \(0\in\operatorname{int}P\), and let \(Q=P^\circ\). Then \(Q\) is a polytope. For each face \(F\) of \(P\), define \(\widehat F=\{x\in Q:\langle x,y\rangle=1\text{ for every }y\in F\}\), with \(\widehat\varnothing=Q\) and \(\widehat P=\varnothing\). Then \(\widehat F\) is a face of \(Q\), \(\dim F+\dim\widehat F=d-1\), and \(F\subseteq G\) implies \(\widehat G\subseteq\widehat F\). Conversely, for every face \(G\) of \(Q\), define \(F=\{y\in P:\langle x,y\rangle=1\text{ for every }x\in G\}\), taking \(F=P\) for \(G=\varnothing\) and \(F=\varnothing\) for \(G=Q\); then \(\widehat F=G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The polar of a polytope containing the origin in its interior is a polytope. Their faces correspond bijectively with inclusion reversed and complementary dimensions summing to d minus one, subject to the stated empty-set and whole-polytope conventions.
assumptions_latex: \dim\varnothing=-1\text{ for the dimension formula on improper faces}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Q\text{ is a polytope, and }F\mapsto\widehat F\text{ is an inclusion-reversing bijection of face lattices with }\dim F+\dim\widehat F=d-1.

children.title: Face-Lattice Reversal
children.top_down_role: Order-reversing correspondence between facial posets of polar partners.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lattice-operation form of face-poset reversal for polar polytopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P\subset\mathbb R^d\) be a full-dimensional polytope with \(0\in\operatorname{int}P\). In the extended face lattices, let \(F\wedge G=F\cap G\), and let \(F\vee G\) be the smallest face containing \(F\cup G\). Polar face duality exchanges these operations:
\[
(F\wedge G)^*=F^*\vee G^*,\qquad
(F\vee G)^*=F^*\wedge G^*.
\]
These formulas include improper faces under \(\varnothing^*=P^\circ\) and \(P^*=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polar face duality exchanges intersections of faces with their lattice joins, including the empty and whole faces.
assumptions_latex: The extended face lattices include the empty and whole faces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((F\wedge G)^*=F^*\vee G^*\) and \((F\vee G)^*=F^*\wedge G^*\) for all faces \(F,G\) of \(P\).

notation.meaning: meet in the extended face lattice
join in the extended face lattice
face of the polar paired with F

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correctly qualified extended-face-lattice duality, including improper faces and involution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P\subset\mathbb R^d\) be a full-dimensional polytope with \(0\in\operatorname{int}P\). For every nonempty proper face \(F\) of \(P\), set
\[
F^*=\{y\in P^\circ:\langle x,y\rangle=1\text{ for every }x\in F\},
\]
and extend the assignment by \(\varnothing^*=P^\circ\) and \(P^*=\varnothing\). Then \(F\mapsto F^*\) is a bijection from the extended face lattice of \(P\) onto that of \(P^\circ\), satisfies
\[
F\subseteq G\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad G^*\subseteq F^*,
\]
and is involutive under \(P^{\circ\circ}=P\): \((F^*)^*=F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polar dualization is an involutive order-reversing bijection between the extended face lattices of a full-dimensional polytope containing zero internally and its polar.
assumptions_latex: The extended face lattices include the empty and whole faces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\mapsto F^*\) is an involutive inclusion-reversing bijection between the extended face lattices of \(P\) and \(P^\circ\).

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\mapsto F^*\) is an inclusion-reversing bijection between the face lattices of \(P\) and \(P^\circ\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combinatorial duality for polytopes containing the origin internally.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every nonempty proper face \(F\) of \(P\), define \(F^*=\{y\in P^\circ:\langle x,y\rangle=1\ \forall x\in F\}\), and set \(\varnothing^*=P^\circ\) and \(P^*=\varnothing\). Then \(F^*\) is a face of \(P^\circ\), the assignment is bijective, and \((F^*)^*=F\) after identifying \(P^{\circ\circ}=P\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Enumerative consequence of complementary dimensions for proper faces of polar polytopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P\subset\mathbb R^d\) be a full-dimensional polytope with \(0\in\operatorname{int}P\), and let \(f_k(P)\) denote the number of \(k\)-dimensional faces of \(P\). Then
\[
f_k(P)=f_{d-1-k}(P^\circ),\qquad k=0,\ldots,d-1.
\]
In particular, vertices of either polytope correspond in number to facets of its polar partner.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polarity reverses the face-number sequence: k-faces of a polytope are counted by complementary-dimensional faces of its polar.
assumptions_latex: \(f_k(P)\) counts the k-dimensional faces of P.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correctly qualified dimension-complementarity formula for paired proper faces of polar polytopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P\subset\mathbb R^d\) be a full-dimensional polytope with \(0\in\operatorname{int}P\). For every nonempty proper face \(F\) of \(P\), define
\[
F^*=\{y\in P^\circ:\langle x,y\rangle=1\text{ for every }x\in F\}.
\]
Then \(F^*\) is a nonempty proper face of \(P^\circ\) and
\[
\dim F+\dim F^*=d-1.
\]
Consequently, \(k\)-faces correspond to \((d-1-k)\)-faces.

children.top_down_role: Containment plus incidence structure retained through order reversal.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Incidence and Chain Reversal under Polytope Polarity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pairwise incidence and chain correspondence for the augmented face lattices of polar polytopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subset\mathbb R^d\) be a full-dimensional polytope with \(0\in\operatorname{int}P\), and let \(P^\circ=\{y:\langle x,y\rangle\le 1\ \forall x\in P\}\). For every face \(F\) of \(P\), set \(F^*=\{y\in P^\circ:\langle x,y\rangle=1\ \forall x\in F\}\), with \(\varnothing^*=P^\circ\) and \(P^*=\varnothing\). Then, for all faces \(F,G\) of \(P\), \[F\subseteq G\iff G^*\subseteq F^*.\] Consequently, every strict face chain \(F_0\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq F_k\) corresponds to the strict reversed chain \(F_k^*\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq F_0^*\) in \(P^\circ\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a full-dimensional polytope containing the origin in its interior, polar duality preserves face incidence while reversing containment, and therefore reverses every strict face chain.
assumptions_latex: \(F,G\) are faces in the augmented face lattice of \(P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\subseteq G\iff G^*\subseteq F^*\), and strict face chains correspond in reverse order.

notation.meaning: Face of the polar dual to F, including the stated improper-face conventions.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under polar face duality, \(F\subseteq G\) holds if and only if \(G^*\subseteq F^*\). Consequently, every incident face pair of \(P\) yields an incident pair of \(P^\circ\) with ranks reversed; chains \(F_0\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq F_k\) correspond to chains \(F_k^*\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq F_0^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polarity preserves face incidence after reversing containment, and it sends every face chain to a reversed chain in the polar.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(Q\in\mathbb S_{++}^d\) be a real symmetric positive-definite matrix and use the standard Euclidean inner product on \(\mathbb R^d\).
