knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The quadratic ellipsoid generated by \(Q\) is \[E_Q:=\{x\in\mathbb R^d:x^\top Qx\le1\}.\] Its Euclidean polar is the inverse-quadratic ellipsoid \[E_Q^\circ=E_{Q^{-1}}:=\{y\in\mathbb R^d:y^\top Q^{-1}y\le1\}.\] Equivalently, if \(E=T B_2\) for an invertible linear map \(T\), then \[E^\circ=T^{-\top}B_2.\]

special_cases_latex: For \(Q=I\), the Euclidean unit ball is self-polar.

children.title: Minkowski Gauge Theory
children.top_down_role: Positively homogeneous convex functionals generated by origin-anchored convex sets and their functional polars.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and convex with \(0\in C\). Adopt \(\inf\varnothing=+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Possibly asymmetric and extended-valued gauges generated by origin-containing convex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Minkowski gauge of \(C\) is \[\gamma_C(x):=\inf\{\lambda\ge0:x\in\lambda C\},\qquad x\in\mathbb R^n.\] A gauge is equivalently a function \(k:\mathbb R^n\to[0,+\infty]\) that is convex, positively homogeneous, and satisfies \(k(0)=0\). Its functional polar is \[k^\circ(y):=\inf\{\mu\ge0:(\forall x)\ \langle x,y\rangle\le\mu k(x)\}.\] When \(k=\gamma_C\), one has \(k^\circ=\gamma_{C^\circ}\) and \(k^{\circ\circ}=\operatorname{cl}k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Minkowski gauge measures the smallest nonnegative dilation of an origin-containing convex set needed to contain a point, with value infinity if no dilation contains it. Gauges are exactly nonnegative convex positively homogeneous functions vanishing at zero. Functional polarity assigns the smallest multiplier controlling the pairing by the gauge; for set-generated gauges it coincides with taking the gauge of the polar set.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Positive homogeneity and convexity are equivalent to positive homogeneity and subadditivity: \(k(x+z)\le k(x)+k(z)\).
For finite definite \(k\), \(k^\circ(y)=\sup_{x\ne0}\langle x,y\rangle/k(x)\).
special_cases_latex: If \(C\) is a cone, \(\gamma_C\) is the indicator of \(C\) with values \(0\) and \(+\infty\).
If \(C\) is a symmetric convex body with \(0\in\operatorname{int}C\), then \(\gamma_C\) is a norm.
immediate_consequences_latex: The polar-gauge inequality is \(\langle x,y\rangle\le k(x)k^\circ(y)\) on the effective domains.
If \(C\) is closed, then \(\gamma_C=\sigma_{C^\circ}\).
boundary_notes: A gauge need not be symmetric or definite and may take the value \(+\infty\).
Closure in \(k^{\circ\circ}=\operatorname{cl}k\) is epigraphical lower-semicontinuous closure.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Basic Properties of the Minkowski Functional
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finiteness, sublinearity, continuity, and level-set recovery for the gauge of a convex neighborhood of the origin.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $X$ be a normed linear space, let $K\subseteq X$ be convex with $0\in\operatorname{int}K$, and let $p_K$ be its Minkowski functional. Then, for all $x,x_1,x_2\in X$ and all $\alpha>0$,
\[
0\le p_K(x)<\infty,\qquad p_K(\alpha x)=\alpha p_K(x),\qquad p_K(x_1+x_2)\le p_K(x_1)+p_K(x_2).
\]
Moreover, $p_K$ is continuous and
\[
\overline K=\{x\in X:p_K(x)\le1\},\qquad \operatorname{int}K=\{x\in X:p_K(x)<1\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Minkowski functional of a convex set containing the origin in its interior is finite and nonnegative everywhere, positively homogeneous, subadditive, and continuous. Its closed unit sublevel set is the closure of K, and its strict unit sublevel set is the interior of K.
assumptions_latex: X\text{ is a normed linear space}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: 0\le p_K(x)<\infty,\quad p_K(\alpha x)=\alpha p_K(x),\quad p_K(x_1+x_2)\le p_K(x_1)+p_K(x_2),\quad p_K\text{ is continuous},\quad \overline K=\{p_K\le1\},\quad \operatorname{int}K=\{p_K<1\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Correspondence Between Closed Gauges and Unit Sets
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Work in \(\mathbb R^n\). Let \(\mathcal C_0\) be the class of nonempty closed convex sets containing \(0\), and let \(\mathcal G_{\mathrm{cl}}\) be the class of closed gauges.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional closed correspondence; without closedness, generating sets are not unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the two maps \[C\in\mathcal C_0\longmapsto\gamma_C(x):=\inf\{\lambda\ge0:x\in\lambda C\},\] and \[k\in\mathcal G_{\mathrm{cl}}\longmapsto U_k:=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:k(x)\le1\}.\] These maps are mutually inverse: \[U_{\gamma_C}=C\quad(C\in\mathcal C_0),\qquad \gamma_{U_k}=k\quad(k\in\mathcal G_{\mathrm{cl}}).\] Hence closed origin-containing convex sets and closed gauges encode the same objects in set and functional form.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed convex set containing the origin determines its gauge, and a closed gauge determines its unit sublevel set. These operations undo each other. The set therefore records all radial unit bounds of the function, while positive homogeneity reconstructs every other sublevel set by scaling.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For every \(\alpha>0\), \(\{x:\gamma_C(x)\le\alpha\}=\alpha C\).
The epigraph is determined by the unit set: \(\operatorname{epi}\gamma_C=\{(x,t):t\ge0,\ x\in tC\}\).
special_cases_latex: Symmetric closed bounded \(C\) with \(0\in\operatorname{int}C\) correspond exactly to norms.
Closed convex cones correspond to indicator gauges taking only \(0\) and \(+\infty\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Set inclusion reverses pointwise gauge order: \(C_1\subseteq C_2\Rightarrow\gamma_{C_2}\le\gamma_{C_1}\).
The effective domain satisfies \(\operatorname{dom}\gamma_C=\operatorname{cone}C\).
boundary_notes: For a nonclosed generator \(C\), the unit sublevel set of \(\gamma_C\) can exceed \(C\); closedness restores exact recovery.
The correspondence allows asymmetric and unbounded generators, so it is broader than norm-unit-ball duality.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Functional reconstruction and positive-sublevel dilation for an extended-valued positively homogeneous function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(p:X\to[0,+\infty]\) be positively homogeneous with \(p(0)=0\), and set
\[
B=\{x\in X:p(x)\le1\}.
\]
Then
\[
p=\gamma_B,
\qquad
\{x:p(x)\le r\}=rB\quad(r>0).
\]
If \(p\) is sublinear, then \(B\) is convex and contains \(0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gauge Unit Set and Homothetic Sublevels
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(k:\mathbb R^n\to[0,+\infty]\) be a gauge and define its unit set \(U:=\operatorname{lev}_{\le1}k=\{x:k(x)\le1\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-valued gauges; exact closed-set recovery is asserted when \(k\) is closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The unit sublevel-set geometry of \(k\) is the set \[U_k:=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:k(x)\le1\}.\] It is convex and contains \(0\), and the gauge is recovered by \[k(x)=\gamma_{U_k}(x)=\inf\{\lambda\ge0:x\in\lambda U_k\}.\] For every \(\alpha>0\), positive homogeneity gives \[\{x:k(x)\le\alpha\}=\alpha U_k.\] If \(k\) is closed, then \(U_k\) is closed and is the unique closed convex origin-containing generator of \(k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The unit sublevel set contains the complete geometry of a gauge. Every positive sublevel set is a homothetic copy of it, and the gauge value of a point is the least scale at which the point enters that unit set. For a closed gauge, the unit set is the unique closed convex set containing the origin that generates the gauge.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(k(x)\le\alpha\Longleftrightarrow x\in\alpha U_k\) for \(\alpha>0\).
\(\operatorname{epi}k=\{(x,t):t\ge0,\ x\in tU_k\}\).
special_cases_latex: If \(k\) is a norm, \(U_k\) is its symmetric closed unit ball.
If \(k=\delta_K\) for a convex cone \(K\), then \(U_k=K\) and every positive sublevel set equals \(K\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Pointwise order becomes reverse unit-set inclusion: \(k_1\le k_2\Rightarrow U_{k_2}\subseteq U_{k_1}\).
Closedness of \(k\) is equivalent to closedness of its epigraph and entails closedness of every sublevel set.
boundary_notes: The zero sublevel set need not equal \(\{0\}\); it records degenerate zero directions.
Negative sublevel levels are empty because a gauge is nonnegative.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and convex with \(0\in C\), and let \(\gamma_C(x)=\inf\{\lambda\ge0:x\in\lambda C\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional raywise absorption for possibly nonabsorbing generators and extended-valued gauges.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A vector \(x\in\mathbb R^n\) is absorbed by \(C\) when \[(\exists\lambda>0)\quad x\in\lambda C.\] The absorbed-direction set is therefore \[\operatorname{Abs}(C):=\bigcup_{\lambda>0}\lambda C=\operatorname{cone}C.\] It is exactly the effective domain of the gauge: \[\operatorname{dom}\gamma_C:=\{x:\gamma_C(x)<+\infty\}=\operatorname{Abs}(C).\] The set \(C\) is absorbing in \(\mathbb R^n\) precisely when \(\operatorname{Abs}(C)=\mathbb R^n\), equivalently when \(\gamma_C\) is finite everywhere.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A direction is absorbed by an origin-containing convex set if some positive dilation of the set contains the direction. All absorbed directions form the conic hull of the set, and this cone is exactly the finite-valued domain of the Minkowski gauge. Thus failure of radial absorption is represented functionally by infinite gauge values outside the absorbed cone.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(x\in\operatorname{dom}\gamma_C\Longleftrightarrow(\exists\lambda>0)\ \lambda^{-1}x\in C\).
In finite dimensions, a convex \(C\) containing \(0\) is absorbing exactly when \(0\in\operatorname{int}C\).
special_cases_latex: If \(C\) contains a neighborhood of \(0\), every direction is absorbed and \(\gamma_C\) is finite.
If \(C\) lies in a proper linear subspace \(L\), then \(\operatorname{dom}\gamma_C\subseteq L\).
immediate_consequences_latex: For \(x\notin\operatorname{cone}C\), \(\gamma_C(x)=+\infty\).
The gauge domain is a convex cone even when \(C\) itself is not a cone.
boundary_notes: Absorption concerns reaching a point after dilation; it does not imply boundedness, symmetry, or definiteness of the gauge.
The equality between absorption and interior inclusion uses the finite-dimensional ambient topology.

notation.meaning: Set of vectors absorbed by positive dilations of \(C\).

notation.meaning: Minkowski gauge of C, with the infimum of the empty set equal to positive infinity.
Set of directions absorbed by positive dilations of C.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard directional-domain characterization of a Minkowski functional; exact source locator pending
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directional absorption is identified with the effective domain of an extended-valued gauge.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The direction \(u\in X\) is absorbed by \(C\) if there exists \(t>0\) such that \(u\in tC\). The directional absorption set is
\[
D_C:=\bigcup_{t>0}tC.
\]
Because \(C\) is convex and contains \(0\), this union is the convex cone generated by \(C\). Moreover,
\[
u\in D_C\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \gamma_C(u)<+\infty,
\]
so \(D_C=\operatorname{cone}(C)=\operatorname{dom}\gamma_C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A direction is absorbed when some positive dilation of the set contains it. Absorbed directions form the generated cone and exactly equal the gauge's finite domain.
knowledge_statements.title: Directional Absorption

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition, cone identity, effective-domain characterization, and content kind are mathematically appropriate, but no inspectable source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Nonabsorbing Direction Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Missing ray coverage associated with infinite gauge values.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Boundary Membership Does Not Determine Gauge Finiteness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Paired planar convex cones realize both possible gauge behaviors at a boundary direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C_1=\mathbb R_+^2\) and \(C_2=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:y>0\}\cup\{0\}\). Both are convex cones and hence \(D_{C_i}=C_i\). For \(u=(1,0)\),
\[
u\in\partial D_{C_1}\cap D_{C_1},\qquad \gamma_{C_1}(u)=0,
\]
whereas
\[
u\in\partial D_{C_2}\setminus D_{C_2},\qquad \gamma_{C_2}(u)=+\infty.
\]
Thus membership in \(\partial D_C\) alone determines neither finiteness nor infiniteness of \(\gamma_C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The same planar boundary direction has zero gauge for a closed absorption cone and infinite gauge for an open-sided absorption cone, so boundary membership alone is inconclusive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: u\in\partial D_{C_1}\cap D_{C_1},\ \gamma_{C_1}(u)=0,\qquad u\in\partial D_{C_2}\setminus D_{C_2},\ \gamma_{C_2}(u)=+\infty.

notation.meaning: Boundary direction used in both examples.

knowledge_statements.title: Boundary Membership Does Not Determine Gauge Finiteness

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a topological real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u\notin D_C\) implies \(\gamma_C(u)=+\infty\), while membership in \(\partial D_C\) alone does not determine whether \(\gamma_C(u)\) is finite.

notation.meaning: Cone of directions absorbed by C.
Topological boundary of the absorption cone.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct boundary consequence of the effective-domain formula for a Minkowski gauge; exact source locator pending
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Describes the topological interface between absorbed and nonabsorbed directions without assuming first countability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(u\in X\),
\[
\gamma_C(u)<+\infty\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad u\in D_C.
\]
Consequently, every \(u\notin D_C\) satisfies \(\gamma_C(u)=+\infty\). The boundary is
\[
\partial D_C=\overline{D_C}\cap\overline{X\setminus D_C},
\]
so every neighborhood of a boundary point meets both absorbed and nonabsorbed directions. A point of \(\partial D_C\) may itself belong to \(D_C\), in which case its gauge is finite; hence boundary membership alone does not imply an infinite gauge.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Outside the absorption cone the gauge is infinite. Every neighborhood of its boundary meets absorbed and nonabsorbed directions, but a boundary point itself may still have finite gauge.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonabsorbing Direction Boundaries

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Reciprocity of Radial Size and Gauge Value
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex with \(0\in C\). For \(u\ne0\), define the radial size \(\rho_C(u):=\sup\{t\ge0:tu\in C\}\), allowing values in \([0,+\infty]\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Raywise extended-value reciprocity; the most direct formula applies when the intersection of \(C\) with the ray is radially closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a direction \(u\ne0\), radial-gauge reciprocity is the extended-real relation \[\gamma_C(u)=\rho_C(u)^{-1},\] with conventions \(1/0=+\infty\) and \(1/(+\infty)=0\), whenever the ray section \(\{t\ge0:tu\in C\}\) is closed at its supremum. More generally, for every \(t>0\), \[\gamma_C(tu)=t\gamma_C(u)=\frac{t}{\rho_C(u)}.\] Equivalently, \(tu\in C\) exactly when \(t\le\rho_C(u)\), while \(tu\in\lambda C\) exactly when \(t\le\lambda\rho_C(u)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The radial function measures how far the generating set extends along a ray, while the gauge measures the dilation needed to reach a point on that ray. These quantities are reciprocal: an absent ray gives radial size zero and infinite gauge, an unbounded ray gives infinite radial size and zero gauge, and a finite positive radial size gives its ordinary reciprocal.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\rho_C(u)=\sup\{t\ge0:\gamma_C(tu)\le1\}\).
For \(\gamma_C(u)\in(0,+\infty)\), the normalized point \(u/\gamma_C(u)\) lies on the radial boundary of a raywise closed \(C\).
special_cases_latex: If \(C\) is a convex body with \(0\in\operatorname{int}C\), then \(0<\rho_C(u)<+\infty\) and \(0<\gamma_C(u)<+\infty\) for every \(u\ne0\).
If the entire ray \(\mathbb R_+u\) lies in \(C\), then \(\rho_C(u)=+\infty\) and \(\gamma_C(u)=0\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Gauge sublevel geometry and radial boundary data determine each other ray by ray.
Positive homogeneity reduces evaluation on a ray to one directional value.
boundary_notes: If \(C\) is not closed along a ray, the supremal radial endpoint need not belong to \(C\); closure qualifications are then necessary for endpoint membership.
The radial function here is direction-dependent and is not the recession function of a convex function.

notation.meaning: Maximum extended radial scale of \(C\) in direction \(u\).

children.title: Radial Functions
children.top_down_role: Raywise size representation of star-shaped or convex sets.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Radial Supremum Does Not Recover a Non-Star-Shaped Ray Section
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp failure of interval recovery when star-shapedness is absent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix \(u\neq0\) and let \(C=\{0,2u\}\). Then \(0\in C\) and \(\rho_C(u)=2\), but
\[
S_C(u)=\{0,2\}\neq[0,2]\quad\text{and}\quad[0,2)\nsubseteq S_C(u).
\]
Thus the radial supremum alone does not recover ray membership unless an interval-producing assumption such as star-shapedness is imposed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the two-point set {0,2u}, radial reach equals 2 although all intermediate positive points are missing, so star-shapedness is necessary for interval recovery.

notation.meaning: Radial parameter set in direction u.
Supremum of the radial parameter set.

knowledge_statements.title: Radial Supremum Does Not Recover a Non-Star-Shaped Ray Section

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ray-section structure for sets star-shaped with respect to the origin, including the endpoint-attainment distinction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(u\in X\), define \(S_C(u):=\{r\geq0:ru\in C\}\). If \(C\) is star-shaped with respect to \(0\), then \(S_C(u)\) is an interval containing \(0\), and
\[
[0,\rho_C(u))\subseteq S_C(u)\subseteq[0,\rho_C(u)].
\]
When \(\rho_C(u)<+\infty\), the right endpoint belongs to \(S_C(u)\) exactly when \(\rho_C(u)u\in C\). Moreover, for every \(\lambda>0\),
\[
\rho_C(\lambda u)=\lambda^{-1}\rho_C(u),
\]
and \(\rho_C(0)=+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a set star-shaped about zero, each ray section is an interval determined by its radial value, possibly excluding its finite endpoint; rescaling the direction inversely rescales radial reach.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq X\) is star-shaped with respect to \(0\).

notation.meaning: Radial section of C in direction u.
Radial reach of C in direction u.

notation.meaning: Radial function of C in direction u.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard radial-function definition in convex and star-shaped geometry; exact source locator pending
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-valued radial parameter along rays based at the origin.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The radial function of \(C\) is the extended-valued map \(\rho_C:X\to[0,+\infty]\) defined by
\[
\rho_C(u):=\sup\{r\geq 0:ru\in C\}.
\]
Because \(0\in C\), the set in the supremum is nonempty. The value \(\rho_C(u)=+\infty\) means that it contains arbitrarily large radial parameters, while \(\rho_C(u)=0\) means that no \(r>0\) satisfies \(ru\in C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The radial function is the supremum of the nonnegative radial parameters for which the corresponding point on a ray belongs to the set.
knowledge_statements.title: Radial Functions

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ray-section structure and contravariant scaling of the radial function for a convex set containing the origin.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(u\in X\), let \(S_C(u):=\{r\geq0:ru\in C\}\). If \(C\) is convex and \(0\in C\), then \(S_C(u)\) is an interval containing \(0\), and
\[
[0,\rho_C(u))\subseteq S_C(u)\subseteq[0,\rho_C(u)].
\]
The right endpoint belongs to \(S_C(u)\) exactly when \(\rho_C(u)u\in C\) for finite \(\rho_C(u)\). Moreover, for every \(\lambda>0\),
\[
\rho_C(\lambda u)=\lambda^{-1}\rho_C(u),
\]
with the usual extended-real conventions, and \(\rho_C(0)=+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex set containing zero meets each ray in an interval determined by its radial value, possibly excluding the finite endpoint; the radial function scales inversely when its direction argument is positively rescaled.

notation.meaning: Radial section of C in direction u.
Radial reach of C in direction u.

children.title: Gauge Ray Profiles
children.top_down_role: Raywise gauge values associated with a generating set.

notation.meaning: Gauge profile along the ray generated by u.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive homogeneity determines every gauge profile along a fixed ray.

source_refs.locator: 8 Convex Functions p. 139
source_refs.source_title: Convex Analysis and Monotone Operator Theory in Hilbert Spaces

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a fixed \(u\in X\), define \(g_u(r):=\gamma_C(ru)\) for \(r>0\). Positive homogeneity gives
\[
g_u(r)=r\gamma_C(u),\qquad r>0.
\]
This equality is interpreted in \([0,+\infty]\), with \(r(+\infty)=+\infty\) for \(r>0\). Thus the profile is linear when \(\gamma_C(u)<+\infty\) and identically infinite on positive radii when \(\gamma_C(u)=+\infty\). Moreover, \(\gamma_C(0)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Along each ray, the gauge scales linearly with positive radius; a nonabsorbed direction has an identically infinite positive-radius profile.
knowledge_statements.title: Gauge Ray Profiles

children.title: Radial–Gauge Reciprocity
children.top_down_role: Reciprocal correspondence between radial size plus gauge magnitude.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp-assumption variant: reciprocal conversion is set-theoretic and does not require convexity or star-shapedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subseteq X\) contain \(0\), and define
\[
\gamma_C(u):=\inf\{t>0:u\in tC\},\qquad
\rho_C(u):=\sup\{r\geq0:ru\in C\}.
\]
Then for every \(u\in X\),
\[
\rho_C(u)=\frac1{\gamma_C(u)},
\]
with \(1/0:=+\infty\) and \(1/(+\infty):=0\). No convexity, closedness, or star-shapedness assumption on \(C\) is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Radial reach and the Minkowski functional are extended reciprocals for any set containing zero; convexity, closedness, and star-shapedness are unnecessary for this identity.
knowledge_statements.title: Convexity-Free Radial–Minkowski Reciprocity

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard reciprocal identity between radial functions and Minkowski gauges; exact source locator pending
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-real reciprocity for a convex generator containing the origin.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(u\in X\),
\[
\rho_C(u)=\frac{1}{\gamma_C(u)},
\]
where
\[
\frac{1}{0}:=+\infty,
\qquad
\frac{1}{+\infty}:=0.
\]
Equivalently, if \(0<\gamma_C(u)<+\infty\), then
\[
\rho_C(u)\gamma_C(u)=1.
\]
The extended reciprocal formulation includes unbounded rays, zero-gauge directions, and nonabsorbed directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The radial reach in each direction is the extended reciprocal of the gauge, including the zero and infinite endpoint cases.
knowledge_statements.title: Radial–Gauge Reciprocity

children.title: Zero–Infinite Reciprocity Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Degenerate ray regimes involving vanishing radial size or infinite gauge values.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closedness Is Essential for the Recession-Cone Characterization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A nonclosed convex generator can have an unbounded radial direction that is not a recession direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
C=\operatorname{conv}\bigl(\mathbb{R}_+e_1\cup\{e_2\}\bigr)\subset\mathbb{R}^2.
\]
Then \(C\) is convex, contains \(0\), and is not closed. Since \(te_1\in C\) for every \(t\ge0\),
\[
\rho_C(e_1)=+\infty,\qquad \gamma_C(e_1)=0.
\]
Nevertheless \(e_1\notin\operatorname{rec}C\): one has \(e_2\in C\), but \(e_2+e_1\notin C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convex hull of the nonnegative horizontal ray and the point e2 has zero gauge and infinite radial reach in direction e1, but e1 is not a recession direction.
assumptions_latex: \(e_1,e_2\) are the standard basis vectors of \(\mathbb{R}^2\).
knowledge_statements.title: Closedness Is Essential for the Recession-Cone Characterization

notation.meaning: Minkowski gauge and radial function generated by C.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: extended-real endpoint cases of radial-gauge reciprocity; exact source locator pending
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies the degenerate endpoints of extended radial-gauge reciprocity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under the extended reciprocal conventions,
\[
\gamma_C(u)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\rho_C(u)=+\infty,
\qquad
\gamma_C(u)=+\infty\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\rho_C(u)=0.
\]
Thus an unbounded radial direction is a zero direction of the gauge, while a direction containing no positive point of \(C\) is an infinite-gauge direction. If \(C\) is additionally closed, then
\[
\gamma_C(u)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad u\in\operatorname{rec}C.
\]
Without closedness, arbitrarily large points on the ray need not imply that \(u\) is a recession direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Infinite radial reach corresponds to zero gauge, while zero radial reach corresponds to infinite gauge. For a closed convex generator, zero-gauge directions are precisely its recession directions.
knowledge_statements.title: Zero–Infinite Reciprocity Boundaries

children.title: Gauge-Generator Closedness Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Closedness correspondence between gauges and their generating unit sets.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and convex with \(0\in C\), and let \(\gamma_C\) be its Minkowski gauge. Let \(k\) be an arbitrary gauge with unit set \(U_k=\{x:k(x)\le1\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional lower-semicontinuous closedness and closed convex generators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The gauge-generator closedness correspondence consists of the implications \[C\text{ closed}\Longrightarrow\gamma_C\text{ closed and }\{x:\gamma_C(x)\le1\}=C,\] and \[k\text{ closed}\Longrightarrow U_k\text{ closed},\quad k=\gamma_{U_k}.\] Consequently, the mutually inverse assignments \(C\mapsto\gamma_C\) and \(k\mapsto U_k\) restrict to a bijection between nonempty closed convex sets containing \(0\) and closed gauges. For every \(\alpha>0\), \[\operatorname{lev}_{\le\alpha}\gamma_C=\alpha C.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closedness is preserved across the set–gauge correspondence. A closed convex origin-containing generator has a closed gauge whose unit sublevel set is exactly the generator. Conversely, a closed gauge has a closed unit set and is precisely the gauge generated by that set. All positive sublevel sets are closed dilations of the unit generator.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Closedness of a gauge means lower semicontinuity, equivalently that \(\operatorname{epi}k\) is closed.
For a gauge \(k\), \(\operatorname{cl}k=\gamma_{\operatorname{cl}U_k}\).
special_cases_latex: For a closed convex cone \(K\), its indicator gauge \(\delta_K\) is closed.
For a norm, closedness is automatic because every finite convex function on \(\mathbb R^n\) is continuous.
immediate_consequences_latex: A closed gauge has a unique closed convex origin-containing generator.
If two closed generators have the same gauge, then the generators are equal.
boundary_notes: A nonclosed generating set need not be recovered exactly from the unit sublevel set of its gauge.
The correspondence is stated in finite dimensions; in general topological vector spaces the relevant lower-semicontinuity topology must be specified.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The gauge functional \(p\) is closed if its epigraph
\[
\operatorname{epi}p:=\{(x,r)\in X\times\mathbb R:p(x)\leq r\}
\]
is closed in \(X\times\mathbb R\). Equivalently, \(p\) is lower semicontinuous, or every sublevel set
\[
\operatorname{lev}_{\leq\alpha}p:=\{x\in X:p(x)\leq\alpha\}
\]
is closed for \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\). For a gauge, positive homogeneity reduces the nonnegative sublevels to scaled copies of its unit sublevel.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A gauge is closed when its epigraph is closed, equivalently when it is lower semicontinuous or all its sublevel sets are closed.
knowledge_statements.title: Closed Gauge Functionals

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closedness and level sets of a gauge
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gauge regularity and exact recovery of positive and zero level geometry from a closed convex generator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be closed and convex with \(0\in C\). Then its gauge \(\gamma(\cdot\mid C)\) is closed. For every \(\lambda>0\), \[\{x:\gamma(x\mid C)\leq\lambda\}=\lambda C,\] and \[\{x:\gamma(x\mid C)=0\}=0^+C.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The gauge of a closed convex set containing the origin is closed. Every positive sublevel set is the correspondingly scaled generator, while the zero level set is exactly the generator's recession cone.

children.title: Closed Convex Generators
children.top_down_role: Closed convex unit sets generating gauge functionals.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a Hausdorff topological real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A closed convex generator is a closed convex set \(C\subseteq X\) satisfying \(0\in C\).

notation.meaning: Closed convex generator containing the origin.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generator means the unit set from which an extended Minkowski gauge is formed.

source_refs.locator: 9 Lower Semicontinuous Convex Functions p. 157

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A closed convex generator is a set \(C\subseteq X\) that is closed, convex, and contains \(0\). It generates the extended Minkowski gauge
\[
\gamma_C(x):=\inf\{t>0:x\in tC\},
\]
where \(\inf\varnothing:=+\infty\). Convexity and origin containment make \(\gamma_C\) sublinear. Closedness makes \(C\) recoverable as the unit sublevel of \(\gamma_C\) and makes \(\gamma_C\) lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed convex generator is a closed convex set containing the origin, viewed as the unit set that generates its Minkowski gauge.
knowledge_statements.title: Closed Convex Generators

children.title: Unit-Sublevel Recovery
children.top_down_role: Canonical recovery of a generator from a closed gauge.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a Hausdorff topological real vector space.
\(C\subseteq X\) is closed, convex, and contains \(0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact recovery for closed convex generators, including nonabsorbing directions.

source_refs.locator: 3.3 Properties of Closed Convex Functions p. 19

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The generator is exactly the unit sublevel of its Minkowski gauge:
\[
C=\{x\in X:\gamma_C(x)\leq1\}.
\]
Conversely, if \(p:X\to[0,+\infty]\) is a lower-semicontinuous sublinear functional and \(C_p:=\{x\in X:p(x)\leq1\}\), then \(C_p\) is closed, convex, contains \(0\), and
\[
\gamma_{C_p}=p.
\]
Thus closed convex generators and closed extended-valued gauges are mutually recoverable through gauge formation and the unit-sublevel operation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed convex generator equals its gauge's unit sublevel; conversely, a lower-semicontinuous sublinear functional is recovered as the gauge of its unit sublevel.
knowledge_statements.title: Unit-Sublevel Recovery

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Topological Closure Can Change an Extended Gauge
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonabsorbing two-dimensional example showing that replacing a convex generator by its topological closure need not preserve its gauge.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\{(0,0)\}\cup\{(u,v)\in\mathbb R^2:v>0\}\). Then \(C\) is convex, contains the origin, and \(\overline C=\{(u,v):v\geq0\}\). Moreover, \[\gamma_C(u,v)=\begin{cases}0,&v>0\text{ or }(u,v)=(0,0),\\+\infty,&v<0\text{ or }(v=0,\ u\ne0),\end{cases}\] whereas \[\gamma_{\overline C}(u,v)=\begin{cases}0,&v\geq0,\\+\infty,&v<0.\end{cases}\] Hence \(\gamma_C\ne\gamma_{\overline C}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonabsorbing convex generator, topological closure can change the gauge: closing the upper open half-plane together with the origin changes missing horizontal directions from infinite gauge to zero gauge.
knowledge_statements.title: Topological Closure Can Change an Extended Gauge

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a topological real vector space.
\(C\subseteq X\) is convex and \(0\in C\), but \(C\) need not be closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{x:\gamma_C(x)<1\}\subseteq C\subseteq\{x:\gamma_C(x)\leq 1\}\), and either inclusion may be strict.

notation.meaning: Minkowski gauge of the possibly nonclosed generator C.
Strict and non-strict unit sublevels of the gauge.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard strict/non-strict unit-sublevel sandwich for a Minkowski functional; exact source locator pending
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shows why unit-sublevel recovery can lose radial-boundary information.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a possibly nonclosed convex generator,
\[
\{x\in X:\gamma_C(x)<1\}\subseteq C\subseteq\{x\in X:\gamma_C(x)\leq 1\}.
\]
Either inclusion may be strict. For \(X=\mathbb R\) and \(C=[0,1]\), the point \(1\) shows that the first inclusion is strict. For \(X=\mathbb R\) and \(C=[0,1)\),
\[
\gamma_C(x)=
\begin{cases}
x,&x\geq 0,\\
+\infty,&x<0,
\end{cases}
\]
and therefore
\[
\{x:\gamma_C(x)\leq 1\}=[0,1]\neq C.
\]
Thus the gauge can forget whether limiting radial boundary points belonged to the original generator.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A possibly nonclosed convex generator lies between the strict and non-strict unit sublevels of its gauge. Either inclusion can be strict, so gauge recovery may lose radial-boundary membership information.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonclosed Generator Boundaries

children.title: Gauge Geometry Regimes
children.top_down_role: Gauge classes distinguished by symmetry, definiteness, domain, and representational structure.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(k:\mathbb R^n\to[0,+\infty]\) be a gauge, let \(U_k=\{x:k(x)\le1\}\), let \(D_k=\operatorname{dom}k\), and let \(Z_k=\{x:k(x)=0\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional classification by domain, symmetry, definiteness, and generator structure; the regimes may overlap unless explicitly incompatible.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The principal gauge geometry regimes are defined by the following predicates: \[\begin{aligned} &\text{finite: }D_k=\mathbb R^n;\qquad \text{definite: }Z_k=\{0\};\\ &\text{symmetric: }k(-x)=k(x)\ (\forall x);\qquad \text{closed: }\operatorname{epi}k\text{ is closed};\\ &\text{polyhedral: }U_k\text{ is polyhedral}.\end{aligned}\] A finite, definite, symmetric gauge is a norm. An asymmetric gauge fails symmetry; a lineality-degenerate gauge has \(Z_k\ne\{0\}\); and a nonabsorbing gauge has \(D_k\ne\mathbb R^n\) and therefore takes \(+\infty\) outside its effective domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gauge regimes are distinguished by four independent geometric questions: whether every direction is absorbed, whether nonzero zero-cost directions exist, whether opposite directions have equal cost, and whether the gauge is closed. Additional representational structure, such as polyhedrality, is read from the unit set. The norm regime occurs when the gauge is finite, symmetric, and definite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[k\text{ is a norm}\Longleftrightarrow D_k=\mathbb R^n,\ Z_k=\{0\},\ k(-x)=k(x)\ (\forall x).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Finiteness is equivalent to \(0\in\operatorname{int}U_k\) for a closed gauge.
Definiteness is equivalent to the unit generator containing no nonzero ray when the generator is closed and convex.
special_cases_latex: A norm belongs simultaneously to the finite, definite, symmetric, and closed regimes.
An indicator of a proper closed convex cone is closed but generally nonfinite and highly degenerate on its domain.
immediate_consequences_latex: Symmetry of \(k\) is equivalent to central symmetry of \(U_k\).
Polyhedrality of \(U_k\) yields a polyhedral gauge.
boundary_notes: Asymmetry does not imply degeneracy or nonfiniteness.
A regime label does not by itself assert differentiability, strict convexity, or smoothness.

children.title: Norm-Generating Gauge Regime
children.top_down_role: The balanced, absorbing, and definite regime.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, closed, convex, and contain \(0\), and let \(\gamma_C\) be its gauge.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional norm regime characterized simultaneously in functional and generating-set language.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The generator \(C\) is in the norm-generating regime when it is centrally symmetric, bounded, and absorbing, equivalently \[C=-C,\qquad C\text{ bounded},\qquad 0\in\operatorname{int}C.\] In that case \(\gamma_C\) is finite everywhere, symmetric, and positive away from the origin, hence is a norm. Conversely, every norm \(\|\cdot\|\) has the unique unit ball \[C=\{x:\|x\|\le1\},\] which is closed, bounded, convex, centrally symmetric, contains \(0\) in its interior, and satisfies \(\gamma_C=\|\cdot\|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed convex set generates a norm exactly when it is a centrally symmetric convex body centered at the origin. Interior inclusion supplies finiteness in every direction, boundedness excludes nonzero zero-cost rays, and central symmetry supplies absolute homogeneity. Every norm is recovered from its closed unit ball in this way.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\gamma_C\text{ is a norm}\Longleftrightarrow C=-C,\ C\text{ is bounded},\ 0\in\operatorname{int}C.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Functionally, \(\gamma_C(x)>0\) for \(x\ne0\), \(\gamma_C(x+z)\le\gamma_C(x)+\gamma_C(z)\), and \(\gamma_C(\lambda x)=|\lambda|\gamma_C(x)\).
Geometrically, \(C\) is a centrally symmetric convex body whose center is the origin.
special_cases_latex: For \(C=B_2\), \(\gamma_C\) is the Euclidean norm.
For \(C=[-1,1]^n\), \(\gamma_C=\|\cdot\|_\infty\); for the cross-polytope, \(\gamma_C=\|\cdot\|_1\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The polar \(C^\circ\) is also norm-generating and its gauge is the dual norm.
The norm topology agrees with the Euclidean topology in finite dimensions.
boundary_notes: Dropping symmetry yields an asymmetric gauge, not a norm.
Dropping boundedness permits nonzero directions with zero gauge; dropping interior inclusion permits infinite values.

notation.meaning: Central symmetry of the generator about the origin.

children.title: Symmetric Gauges
children.top_down_role: Gauge geometry invariant under sign reversal.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p\) is symmetric exactly when \(p(-x)=p(x)\) for every \(x\in X\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The gauge \(p\) is symmetric if
\[
p(-x)=p(x)
\]
for every \(x\in X\). Its unit sublevel \(C_p:=\{x\in X:p(x)\leq1\}\) is then centrally symmetric, meaning \(C_p=-C_p\). Conversely, if \(C\subseteq X\) contains \(0\) and satisfies \(C=-C\), then its Minkowski gauge satisfies \(\gamma_C(-x)=\gamma_C(x)\) for every \(x\in X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A gauge is symmetric when it is even. This is equivalent to central symmetry of its unit sublevel or generating set.
knowledge_statements.title: Symmetric Gauges

source_witnesses.locator: 8 Convex Functions p. 139
source_witnesses.source_title: Convex Analysis and Monotone Operator Theory in Hilbert Spaces

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic functional consequences of evenness for finite real gauges; definiteness is not assumed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a real vector space and let \(p:X\to[0,\infty)\) be a finite gauge. If \(p(-x)=p(x)\) for every \(x\in X\), then \(p(\alpha x)=|\alpha|p(x)\) for every \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\), so \(p\) is a seminorm. Its null set \(N=\{x\in X:p(x)=0\}\) is a linear subspace, and \(\bar p(x+N):=p(x)\) is a norm on \(X/N\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every finite symmetric gauge is a seminorm. Its zero set is a linear subspace, and the induced functional on the quotient by that subspace is a norm.
assumptions_latex: \(p:X\to[0,\infty)\) is finite, subadditive, and positively homogeneous for nonnegative scalars.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p\) is a seminorm, \(N=\{p=0\}\) is a linear subspace, and \(\bar p\) is a norm on \(X/N\).
knowledge_statements.title: Symmetric Finite Gauges Are Seminorms

children.title: Definite Gauges
children.top_down_role: Gauge geometry with no nonzero zero-cost directions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definiteness excludes nonzero directions having zero gauge.

source_refs.locator: 10 Convex Functions: Variants p. 177
source_refs.source_title: Convex Analysis and Monotone Operator Theory in Hilbert Spaces

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The gauge \(p\) is definite if
\[
Z(p):=\{x\in X:p(x)=0\}=\{0\}.
\]
Equivalently, \(p(x)>0\) for every nonzero \(x\in X\), where \(+\infty>0\). If \(p=\gamma_C\) for a closed convex generator \(C\), definiteness is equivalent to
\[
\operatorname{rec}C=\{0\}.
\]
Definiteness alone does not make \(p\) a norm: finiteness on all of \(X\) and symmetry are also required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A gauge is definite when only the zero vector has gauge zero. For a closed convex generator this means that its recession cone is trivial, but definiteness alone does not ensure a norm.
knowledge_statements.title: Definite Gauges

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be finite-dimensional and let \(C\subset X\) be nonempty, closed, convex, and contain \(0\). Then \[\gamma_C\text{ is definite}\iff\operatorname{rec}C=\{0\}\iff C\text{ is bounded}.\] No absorption or central-symmetry assumption is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a closed convex generator in finite dimensions, its gauge is definite exactly when the generator is bounded.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset X\) is nonempty, closed, convex, and contains \(0\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional proper lower-semicontinuous gauges and their polar gauges.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p:X\to[0,+\infty]\) be a proper lower-semicontinuous gauge on a finite-dimensional space, and let \(p^\circ\) be its polar gauge. Then \[p\text{ is definite}\iff p^\circ(y)<+\infty\quad\text{for every }y\in X^*.\] Equivalently, definiteness of \(p\) is dual to global finiteness of its polar gauge.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed finite-dimensional gauge is definite exactly when its polar gauge is finite everywhere.
knowledge_statements.title: Definiteness–Polar Finiteness Equivalence

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a finite-dimensional real vector space and let \(C\subset X\) be closed, convex, bounded, centrally symmetric, with \(0\in\operatorname{int}C\). Define \(\gamma_C(x)=\inf\{t>0:x\in tC\}\). Then \(\gamma_C\) is finite, subadditive, absolutely homogeneous, and positive definite; hence it is a norm on \(X\). Moreover, \(C=\{x\in X:\gamma_C(x)\leq 1\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed, bounded, symmetric convex body containing zero in its interior generates a norm, and the body is exactly that norm's unit ball.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the norm specialization of a gauge and gives its equivalent positivity, triangle-inequality, and absolute-homogeneity characterization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A gauge \(k\) on \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is a norm if it is finite everywhere, symmetric, and positive away from the origin. Equivalently, \(k:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) satisfies \(k(x)>0\) for every \(x\ne0\), \(k(x_1+x_2)\le k(x_1)+k(x_2)\) for all \(x_1,x_2\), and \(k(\lambda x)=|\lambda|k(x)\) for all \(x\) and all \(\lambda\in\mathbb{R}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A norm is exactly a gauge that is finite everywhere, symmetric, and positive except at zero. Equivalently, it is a real-valued positive-definite function satisfying the triangle inequality and absolute homogeneity.
assumptions_latex: k\text{ is a gauge on }\mathbb{R}^n\text{ for the specialization definition}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Norm on a Real Vector Space
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of a finite real-valued norm by positive definiteness, absolute homogeneity, and the triangle inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \mathbb{E} be a real vector space. A function \|\cdot\|:\mathbb{E}\to\mathbb{R} is a norm if, for all \mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{E} and \lambda\in\mathbb{R}, (i) \|\mathbf{x}\|\geq 0 and \|\mathbf{x}\|=0\iff \mathbf{x}=0; (ii) \|\lambda\mathbf{x}\|=|\lambda|\,\|\mathbf{x}\|; and (iii) \|\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{y}\|\leq \|\mathbf{x}\|+\|\mathbf{y}\|.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A norm on a real vector space is a real-valued function that is nonnegative and vanishes only at zero, is absolutely homogeneous, and satisfies the triangle inequality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \|\cdot\|\text{ is a norm when it satisfies positive definiteness, absolute homogeneity, and the triangle inequality.}

children.title: Lineality-Degenerate Gauge Regimes
children.top_down_role: Gauges with nontrivial zero directions.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex with \(0\in C\), and let \(k=\gamma_C\). Denote the recession cone of \(C\) by \(0^+C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed finite-dimensional gauges; zero directions may form a cone that is not a linear subspace unless symmetry is imposed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The zero cone of \(k\) is \[Z(k):=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:k(x)=0\}.\] For a closed generator, \[Z(k)=0^+C.\] The gauge is lineality-degenerate when \(Z(k)\ne\{0\}\), equivalently when \(C\) contains a nonzero recession direction. Its two-sided lineality subspace is \[L(k):=Z(k)\cap(-Z(k))=(0^+C)\cap(-0^+C).\] Along every \(z\in L(k)\), one has \(k(x+z)=k(x)\) whenever both sides are interpreted on the effective domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed gauge is degenerate when it assigns zero to a nonzero direction. The complete cone of such directions is the recession cone of its unit generator. Directions that occur together with their negatives form the lineality subspace; translation along this subspace leaves the gauge unchanged. For asymmetric gauges, the zero cone may be one-sided and therefore need not itself be a subspace.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(z\in Z(k)\Longleftrightarrow k(tz)=0\) for every \(t\ge0\).
For a symmetric gauge, \(Z(k)=L(k)\) is a linear subspace.
special_cases_latex: If \(C\) is bounded, then \(0^+C=\{0\}\), so the gauge is definite.
If \(C=K\) is a closed convex cone, then \(k=\delta_K\) and \(Z(k)=K\).
immediate_consequences_latex: A norm has no nonzero zero directions.
Quotienting a symmetric finite gauge by its zero subspace yields a definite gauge on the quotient space.
boundary_notes: The term lineality-degenerate should not obscure one-sided degeneracy: \(Z(k)\) may strictly contain \(L(k)\).
Zero directions concern unboundedness of the generator, whereas infinite values concern failure of absorption.

notation.meaning: Two-sided lineality subspace of the zero cone.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A seminorm gauge on a real vector space \(X\) is a finite function \(p:X\to[0,\infty)\) such that \(p(x+y)\leq p(x)+p(y)\) and \(p(\alpha x)=|\alpha|p(x)\) for all \(x,y\in X\) and \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\). Its kernel \(\ker p=\{x\in X:p(x)=0\}\) is a vector subspace, and the seminorm is a norm exactly when \(\ker p=\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A seminorm gauge is subadditive and absolutely homogeneous but may vanish on an entire nonzero subspace.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite sublinear gauge \(q\), define \[L_q=\{\ell:q(\ell)=q(-\ell)=0\}.\] Then \(L_q\) is a vector subspace, \(q(x+\ell)=q(x)\) for all \(x\) and \(\ell\in L_q\), and every translation-invariance subspace is contained in \(L_q\). knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p\) be a seminorm on a real vector space \(X\), and set \(L=\ker p\). Then \(L\) is a vector subspace and \(p(x+\ell)=p(x)\) for every \(x\in X\) and \(\ell\in L\). Conversely, if a vector subspace \(M\subset X\) satisfies \(p(x+m)=p(x)\) for all \(x\in X\) and \(m\in M\), then \(M\subset L\). knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p\) be a seminorm on a real vector space \(X\), let \(L=\ker p\), and write elements of the quotient as \(x+L\). The formula \(\bar p(x+L)=p(x)\) is independent of the representative because \(p(x+\ell)=p(x)\) for \(\ell\in L\). knowledge_statements.statement_title: Extended-Valued Gauge of a Nonabsorbing Generator
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and convex with \(0\in C\), and define \(k=\gamma_C\) using \(\inf\varnothing=+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional generators that do not absorb the entire ambient space; gauges are allowed to be proper extended-real-valued functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The generator \(C\) is nonabsorbing when \[\bigcup_{\lambda>0}\lambda C\ne\mathbb R^n.\] Its gauge is then extended-valued with effective domain \[\operatorname{dom}k=\{x:k(x)<+\infty\}=\bigcup_{\lambda>0}\lambda C=\operatorname{cone}C\subsetneq\mathbb R^n,\] and \[k(x)=+\infty\qquad(x\notin\operatorname{cone}C).\] Conversely, \(k\) is finite everywhere if and only if \(C\) is absorbing; for convex \(C\) in finite dimensions this is equivalent to \(0\in\operatorname{int}C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonabsorbing generator misses at least one ambient direction under every finite positive dilation. Its Minkowski gauge therefore takes the value infinity in each missed direction. The finite-valued domain is exactly the conic hull of the generator, so nonabsorption is equivalent to that domain being a proper convex cone rather than the whole space.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(x\notin\operatorname{dom}\gamma_C\Longleftrightarrow(\forall\lambda>0)\ x\notin\lambda C\).
For closed convex \(C\), nonabsorption is equivalent to \(0\notin\operatorname{int}C\).
special_cases_latex: If \(C\) is contained in a proper subspace \(L\), then \(\gamma_C(x)=+\infty\) for every \(x\notin L\).
If \(C=K\) is a proper convex cone, then \(\gamma_C=0\) on \(K\) and \(+\infty\) outside \(K\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The effective domain of every gauge is a convex cone.
Extended values encode unreachable directions independently of zero-valued recession directions.
boundary_notes: Nonabsorption does not imply that the gauge is improper: it remains proper because \(k(0)=0\) and never takes \(-\infty\).
A generator may be absorbing yet unbounded, producing a finite but degenerate gauge.

notation.meaning: Set on which the extended-valued gauge is finite.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex generators; certificate expressed by a supporting functional at the origin.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be finite-dimensional and let \(C\subset X\) be convex with \(0\in C\). The set \(C\) is nonabsorbing if and only if there exists a nonzero linear functional \(y\in X^*\) such that \[\langle y,c\rangle\leq0\quad\text{for every }c\in C.\] Every \(x\) with \(\langle y,x\rangle>0\) then lies outside \(tC\) for every \(t>0\), so \(\gamma_C(x)=+\infty\).

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\text{ is nonabsorbing}\iff\exists y\in X^*\setminus\{0\}:\sup_{c\in C}\langle y,c\rangle\leq0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In \(\mathbb R^2\), let \[C=\{0\}\cup\{(u,v):v>0,\ u^2+v^2<1\}.\] Then \(C\) is convex, contains \(0\), and \(\operatorname{dom}\gamma_C=\{0\}\cup\{(u,v):v>0\}\). knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(C=\{x\in X:\langle a_i,x\rangle\leq 1,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\). Its Minkowski gauge has the finite maximum representation \[\gamma_C(x)=\inf\{t>0:x\in tC\}=\max_{1\leq i\leq m}\langle a_i,x\rangle.\] Consequently, \(\gamma_C\) is convex, positively homogeneous, finite-valued, and piecewise linear. On every region where one fixed index attains the maximum, the gauge agrees with the corresponding linear functional.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The gauge of an absorbing polytope is the maximum of its normalized facet functionals, hence is finite, convex, positively homogeneous, and piecewise linear.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimality and domain certificates for the vertex-form gauge linear program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(V=[v_1\ \cdots\ v_n]\), the dual of the vertex-form gauge program is \[\sup\{\langle y,x\rangle:V^Ty\leq\mathbf1\}.\] If \(V\lambda=x\), \(\lambda\geq0\), \(V^Ty\leq\mathbf1\), and \(\mathbf1^T\lambda=\langle y,x\rangle\), then \(\lambda\) and \(y\) certify \(\gamma_C(x)\). If the primal is infeasible, equivalently \(x\notin\operatorname{cone}\{v_j\}\), there exists \(y\) with \(V^Ty\leq0\) and \(\langle y,x\rangle>0\), certifying \(\gamma_C(x)=+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Matching feasible primal and dual solutions certify a finite vertex-form gauge value, while a Farkas separator certifies that the gauge is infinite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Primal-dual equality certifies a finite value, and \(V^Ty\leq0<\langle y,x\rangle\) certifies \(\gamma_C(x)=+\infty\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Set \(a_0=0\) and suppose \(\gamma_C(x)=\max_{0\leq i\leq m}\langle a_i,x\rangle\). For \(I(x)=\{i:\langle a_i,x\rangle=\gamma_C(x)\}\), \[\partial\gamma_C(x)=\operatorname{conv}\{a_i:i\in I(x)\}.\] Thus an index \(i\in I(x)\), together with the inequalities \(\langle a_k,x\rangle\leq\langle a_i,x\rangle\) for every \(k\), certifies the evaluated gauge value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The subdifferential of a finite-maximum polyhedral gauge is the convex hull of its active linear pieces, and any maximizing piece certifies the value.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polyhedral polarity for an absorbing polyhedron; unlike the bounded case, the zero vector may be an essential polar vertex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\{x\in\mathbb R^d:\langle a_i,x\rangle\leq1,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\) and suppose \(0\in\operatorname{int}C\). Then \[C^\circ=\operatorname{conv}\bigl(\{0,a_1,\ldots,a_m\}\bigr),\qquad \gamma_C(x)=\sigma_{C^\circ}(x)=\max\{0,\langle a_1,x\rangle,\ldots,\langle a_m,x\rangle\}.\] If \(C\) is bounded, then \(0\in\operatorname{conv}\{a_1,\ldots,a_m\}\), so the zero term is redundant and the seed's facet-maximum formula is recovered.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\operatorname{conv}\{0,v_1,\ldots,v_n\}\subset\mathbb R^d\). Then \[\gamma_C(x)=\inf\left\{\sum_{j=1}^n\lambda_j:\sum_{j=1}^n\lambda_jv_j=x,\ \lambda_j\geq0\right\}.\] The value is \(+\infty\) exactly when \(x\notin\operatorname{cone}\{v_1,\ldots,v_n\}\); whenever it is finite, the minimum is attained.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E=\mathbb{R}^n\). A gauge is an extended-real-valued, nonnegative, convex, positively homogeneous function \(\gamma:E\to[0,+\infty]\) with \(\gamma(0)=0\). Its unit set is \(C_\gamma=\{x\in E:\gamma(x)\le 1\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional extended-valued gauges are covered; symmetry, definiteness, and finiteness are not required.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A gauge \(\gamma:E\to[0,+\infty]\) is polyhedral when its epigraph \(\operatorname{epi}\gamma=\{(x,t)\in E\times\mathbb{R}:\gamma(x)\le t\}\) is a polyhedral convex cone. Equivalently, \(\gamma\) is closed and its unit set \(C_\gamma\) is a polyhedral convex set containing \(0\). Equivalently, there exist finitely many vectors \(a_1,\ldots,a_p\in E\) and a polyhedral cone \(K\subseteq E\) such that \[\gamma(x)=\max_{1\le i\le p}\langle a_i,x\rangle+\delta_K(x),\] with the maximum nonnegative on \(K\). If \(C\subseteq E\) is nonempty, closed, convex, polyhedral, and contains \(0\), then its Minkowski functional \[\gamma_C(x)=\inf\{t\ge0:x\in tC\}\] is a polyhedral gauge, with value \(+\infty\) when no such \(t\) exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polyhedral gauge on a finite-dimensional space is a nonnegative positively homogeneous convex function whose epigraph is a polyhedral cone. For a closed gauge this is equivalent to its unit sublevel set being a polyhedral convex set containing the origin. It can be represented on a polyhedral conic domain as the maximum of finitely many linear functionals. Conversely, the Minkowski functional of any closed polyhedral convex set containing the origin is a polyhedral gauge, possibly taking infinity outside the cone generated by that set.

children.title: Matrix-Invariant Gauge Family
children.top_down_role: Gauge families invariant under matrix symmetry groups.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathbb{S}^n\) be the real symmetric matrices with trace pairing \(\langle X,Y\rangle=\operatorname{tr}(XY)\), let \(\mathbb{O}^n\) be the orthogonal group, and let \(\lambda(X)\in\mathbb{R}^n\) list the eigenvalues of \(X\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definition concerns real symmetric matrices and invariance under orthogonal similarity. Rectangular unitarily invariant gauges require a singular-value formulation not asserted here.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A matrix gauge \(\Gamma:\mathbb{S}^n\to[0,+\infty]\) is orthogonally invariant when \[\Gamma(U^{\mathsf T}XU)=\Gamma(X)\qquad(\forall X\in\mathbb{S}^n)(\forall U\in\mathbb{O}^n).\] Such a gauge is spectral: there is a permutation-invariant gauge \(g:\mathbb{R}^n\to[0,+\infty]\) satisfying \(g(Px)=g(x)\) for every permutation matrix \(P\), such that \[\Gamma(X)=g(\lambda(X)).\] Conversely, every permutation-invariant gauge \(g\) defines an orthogonally invariant matrix gauge by this formula. Its unit set is invariant under orthogonal similarity and equals \(\{X:g(\lambda(X))\le1\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An orthogonally invariant matrix gauge on real symmetric matrices is a gauge whose value is unchanged by orthogonal similarity transformations. It is equivalently a spectral gauge obtained by applying a permutation-invariant vector gauge to the eigenvalue vector. Conversely, a permutation-invariant vector gauge induces an orthogonally invariant gauge. Thus the family is classified by symmetric vector gauges, while its unit sets are precisely the convex gauge unit sets stable under orthogonal similarity.
assumptions_latex: \(\Gamma:\mathbb{S}^n\to[0,+\infty]\) is convex, nonnegative, positively homogeneous, and \(\Gamma(0)=0\).
\(\lambda(X)\) is ordered by a fixed convention, while \(g\) is invariant under coordinate permutations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Gamma(U^{\mathsf T}XU)=\Gamma(X)\) for all \(X,U\), equivalently \(\Gamma=g\circ\lambda\) for a permutation-invariant gauge \(g\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: The unit set \(C_\Gamma=\{X:\Gamma(X)\le1\}\) satisfies \(U^{\mathsf T}C_\Gamma U=C_\Gamma\) for every \(U\in\mathbb{O}^n\).
\(g(x)=\Gamma(\operatorname{Diag}x)\) is permutation invariant and recovers \(\Gamma\) through eigenvalues.
special_cases_latex: If \(g(x)=\|x\|_\infty\), then \(\Gamma(X)=\max_i|\lambda_i(X)|\), the spectral norm on \(\mathbb{S}^n\).
If \(g(x)=\|x\|_1\), then \(\Gamma(X)=\sum_i|\lambda_i(X)|\), the nuclear norm on \(\mathbb{S}^n\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Closedness and convexity of \(\Gamma\) are equivalent to closedness and convexity of its diagonal restriction \(g\).
The polar of a closed invariant gauge is again invariant under the same orthogonal group.
boundary_notes: Permutation invariance alone does not impose sign invariance, so the resulting gauge need not be a norm.
For general rectangular matrices, left-right orthogonal invariance is represented through singular values rather than eigenvalues.

notation.meaning: Eigenvalue vector of a real symmetric matrix.
Group of real orthogonal n-by-n matrices.

children.title: Gauge Calculus
children.top_down_role: Constructions and transformations preserving gauge structure.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Sections 15–16: Polars of Convex Functions and Dual Operations

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E_i\) and \(F\) be finite-dimensional real vector spaces. A gauge is a function into \([0,+\infty]\) that is nonnegative, convex, positively homogeneous, and zero at the origin.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The entry defines the standard finite-dimensional calculus generated by positive combinations, maxima, linear pullbacks, and linear infimal images. Closedness of an infimal image requires separate qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Gauge calculus is the family of operations that sends gauges to gauges. For gauges \(\gamma_i:E\to[0,+\infty]\), coefficients \(\alpha_i\ge0\), and a linear map \(A:E\to F\), the basic constructions are \[\gamma_\Sigma(x)=\sum_i\alpha_i\gamma_i(x),\qquad \gamma_\vee(x)=\max_i\gamma_i(x),\qquad (\eta\circ A)(x)=\eta(Ax),\] and the quotient or infimal image \[(A\gamma)(y)=\inf\{\gamma(x):Ax=y\},\qquad\inf\varnothing=+\infty.\] The first three are gauges whenever their inputs are gauges. The infimal image is a gauge provided it never takes \(-\infty\), which is automatic for nonnegative gauges; it may require lower-semicontinuous closure to be a closed gauge.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gauge calculus consists of operations preserving nonnegative convex positive homogeneity. Nonnegative weighted sums and pointwise maxima of gauges are gauges. Pulling a gauge back through a linear map also produces a gauge. Pushing a gauge forward through a linear map is defined by minimizing over each fiber; because gauges are nonnegative, the result is an extended-valued gauge, although it may fail to be closed without an additional closed-image condition. These constructions include restrictions, quotients, products, intersections of unit sets, and infimal decompositions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma_\Sigma,\gamma_\vee,\eta\circ A\), and \(A\gamma\) are extended-valued gauges, with closure applied to \(A\gamma\) when a closed gauge is required.
equivalent_formulations_latex: At the epigraph level, nonnegative scaling, intersection, inverse linear image, and linear projection are the corresponding convex-cone operations.
For \(C_i=\{x:\gamma_i(x)\le1\}\), \(\{x:\gamma_\vee(x)\le1\}=\bigcap_i C_i\).
special_cases_latex: Taking \(A\) to be an inclusion gives restriction of a gauge to a subspace.
Taking \(A\) to be a coordinate projection gives a quotient gauge.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every construction remains positively homogeneous of degree one.
Extended values are retained when the relevant unit set is nonabsorbing.
boundary_notes: Pointwise minima of gauges are generally not convex and hence are not basic gauge-preserving operations.
A linear infimal image of a closed gauge need not be closed unless an image-closedness condition holds.

notation.meaning: Infimal image of gamma through the linear map A.

children.title: Gauge Combination Calculus

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E\) be finite dimensional, let \(\gamma_i:E\to[0,+\infty]\) be gauges, and put \(C_i=\{x:\gamma_i(x)\le1\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite combinations on a common space are covered. Closure is stated explicitly where infimal convolution may not be lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The canonical finite gauge combinations are the maximum, the nonnegative weighted sum, and the infimal convolution: \[\gamma_\vee(x)=\max_i\gamma_i(x),\qquad \gamma_\Sigma(x)=\sum_i\alpha_i\gamma_i(x)\quad(\alpha_i\ge0),\] \[\gamma_\square(x)=\inf\Big\{\sum_i\gamma_i(x_i):\sum_i x_i=x\Big\}.\] Each is an extended-valued gauge. Their unit-set interpretations include \[C_{\gamma_\vee}=\bigcap_i C_i,\qquad C_{\gamma_\square}=\operatorname{conv}\Big(\bigcup_i C_i\Big)\] whenever the displayed convex hull is closed; otherwise \(C_{\operatorname{cl}\gamma_\square}=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(\bigcup_iC_i)\). Thus maximum corresponds to intersection, while infimal convolution corresponds to convex-hull aggregation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gauge combination calculus combines gauges on one space without losing convexity or positive homogeneity. The pointwise maximum has the intersection of the unit sets as its unit set. A nonnegative weighted sum is again a gauge. Infimal convolution minimizes the sum of component gauges over all decompositions of a vector and corresponds, after closure when necessary, to the convex hull of the component unit sets. These constructions are distinct: maximum enforces all component bounds, weighted sum penalizes them jointly, and infimal convolution permits allocation among components.
assumptions_latex: \(\gamma_i:E\to[0,+\infty]\) are gauges and the index set is finite.
For the unclosed unit-set identity of \(\gamma_\square\), \(\operatorname{conv}(\bigcup_iC_i)\) is closed.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\gamma_\square\) is the greatest gauge majorized by every \(\gamma_i\), up to lower-semicontinuous closure.
\(\gamma_\vee=\gamma_{\cap_iC_i}\) for closed gauge unit sets.
special_cases_latex: For two gauges, \((\gamma_1\square\gamma_2)(x)=\inf_{u+v=x}\{\gamma_1(u)+\gamma_2(v)\}\).
If all \(\gamma_i\) are finite, \(\gamma_\Sigma\) and \(\gamma_\vee\) are finite.
immediate_consequences_latex: Combination unit sets remain convex and contain the origin.
If the inputs are polyhedral, these finite combinations are polyhedral.
boundary_notes: The pointwise minimum \(\min_i\gamma_i\) is generally not convex.
The weighted-sum unit set does not generally equal a Minkowski sum or intersection of the individual unit sets.

notation.meaning: Unit sublevel set of a gauge.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_m\) be gauges and let \(w_i>0\). Then \[\Gamma(x)=\sum_{i=1}^m w_i\gamma_i(x)\] is a gauge with unit set \[C_\Gamma=\left\{x:\sum_{i=1}^m w_i\gamma_i(x)\leq1\right\}.\] Its effective domain is \(\bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{dom}\gamma_i\). If every \(\gamma_i\) is lower semicontinuous, then \(\Gamma\) is lower semicontinuous. If at least one component gauge is definite, then \(\Gamma(x)=0\) implies \(x=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite positive weighted sum of gauges is a gauge; its domain is the intersection of the component domains, while closedness and definiteness inherit under the stated conditions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the star-shaped-set operation representing pointwise addition of gauges, including its zero-scaling convention and convex terminology.

The operation is called the inverse sum; for convex \(\Omega_1\) and \(\Omega_2\), it is called convolution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The inverse sum is the closure of the union of intersections formed from complementary scalings of two star-shaped sets. Its gauge is the sum of their gauges; for convex sets the operation is called convolution.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Polarization reverses the two basic unit-set combinations: \[(\operatorname{conv}(C_1\cup C_2))^\circ=C_1^\circ\cap C_2^\circ,\qquad (C_1\cap C_2)^\circ=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(C_1^\circ\cup C_2^\circ).\] Hence infimal convolution of primal gauges, whose unit set is \(\operatorname{conv}(C_1\cup C_2)\), corresponds to intersection on the polar side, while pointwise maximum of primal gauges corresponds to closed convex-hull combination on the polar side.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polarity exchanges convex hull of a union with intersection, while intersection polarizes to the closed convex hull of the polar sets.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Functional Polar Form of Gauge Combinations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Functional polar-gauge counterparts of the two accepted unit-set polarity identities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C_1,C_2\) be closed convex subsets of a finite-dimensional space containing \(0\), let \(\gamma_i=\gamma_{C_i}\), and define \(\gamma_i^\circ(y)=\sup\{\langle y,x\rangle:\gamma_i(x)\leq1\}\). Then
\[
(\gamma_1\square\gamma_2)^\circ=\max\{\gamma_1^\circ,\gamma_2^\circ\},
\qquad
(\max\{\gamma_1,\gamma_2\})^\circ=\operatorname{cl}(\gamma_1^\circ\square\gamma_2^\circ),
\]
where \(\operatorname{cl}\) denotes the lower-semicontinuous hull. The closure in the second identity cannot be omitted without an additional exactness condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polarization converts primal infimal convolution into a maximum of polar gauges, while the polar of a primal maximum is the closed infimal convolution of the polar gauges.
assumptions_latex: \(C_1,C_2\) are closed convex sets containing \(0\) in a finite-dimensional real vector space.
\(\gamma_i=\gamma_{C_i}\), and functional polarity is defined by support over the gauge unit set.

notation.meaning: lower-semicontinuous hull of a convex function

children.title: Closedness of Infimal Constructions
children.top_down_role: Attainment plus closure issues for infimally generated gauges.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma_1\square\gamma_2\) is finite and lower semicontinuous, and every defining infimum is attained.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Coercivity means that every sublevel set of each \(\gamma_i\) is bounded; together with lower semicontinuity, this makes the unit sets \(C_1\) and \(C_2\) compact. Consequently, \(\operatorname{conv}(C_1\cup C_2)\) is compact, and \[h(x)=\inf_{x_1+x_2=x}\bigl(\gamma_1(x_1)+\gamma_2(x_2)\bigr)=\gamma_{\operatorname{conv}(C_1\cup C_2)}(x)\] is a finite lower-semicontinuous gauge. For every \(x\in X\), the displayed infimum is attained by at least one decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In finite dimensions, lower semicontinuity and coercivity make the unit sets compact, ensuring that the infimal gauge is closed and its infimum is attained.
knowledge_statements.title: Closedness of Infimal Constructions

source_witnesses.locator: 3.4 A Study of the Infimal Convolution p. 119

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact finite-dimensional criterion separating lower semicontinuity and attainment for an infimal convolution of closed gauges.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h=\gamma_1\square\gamma_2\), where \[h(x)=\inf_{u+v=x}\bigl(\gamma_1(u)+\gamma_2(v)\bigr).\] Then \[\operatorname{epi}\gamma_1+\operatorname{epi}\gamma_2\subseteq\operatorname{epi}h,\qquad \overline{\operatorname{epi}\gamma_1+\operatorname{epi}\gamma_2}=\operatorname{epi}(\operatorname{cl}h).\] Moreover, \(\operatorname{epi}\gamma_1+\operatorname{epi}\gamma_2\) is closed if and only if \(h\) is lower semicontinuous and its defining infimum is attained at every \(x\) where \(h(x)<+\infty\). In that case, \[\operatorname{epi}h=\operatorname{epi}\gamma_1+\operatorname{epi}\gamma_2.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The epigraph sum is closed exactly when the infimal gauge is lower semicontinuous and every finite infimum is attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{epi}\gamma_1+\operatorname{epi}\gamma_2\text{ is closed}\iff h\text{ is lower semicontinuous and every finite defining infimum is attained}.

notation.meaning: infimal convolution of the two gauges

knowledge_statements.title: Epigraph-Sum Closedness Criterion

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closed Gauges with Nonclosed Infimal Convolution
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional cone example showing that separate closedness of the input gauges does not ensure closedness of their infimal convolution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=\mathbb S^2\), let \(K=\mathbb S^2_+\), and let \(L=\operatorname{span}\{E_{22}\}\). The indicator gauges \(\gamma_1=\delta_K\) and \(\gamma_2=\delta_L\) are proper and lower semicontinuous, but \[\gamma_1\square\gamma_2=\delta_{K+L}.\] Writing matrices as \(\begin{psmallmatrix}a&b\\b&c\end{psmallmatrix}\), one has \[K+L=\left\{a>0\right\}\cup\left\{a=0,\ b=0\right\},\] with the entry \(c\) unrestricted. Hence \(K+L\) is not closed: \(\begin{psmallmatrix}1/n&1\\1&0\end{psmallmatrix}\in K+L\) converges to \(\begin{psmallmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{psmallmatrix}\notin K+L\). Thus the infimal convolution of two closed gauges need not be lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Indicators of the positive-semidefinite cone and a one-dimensional matrix subspace are closed gauges whose infimal convolution is the indicator of a nonclosed cone sum.
assumptions_latex: \(X=\mathbb S^2\) with its usual finite-dimensional topology.

notation.meaning: matrix having one in entry \((2,2)\) and zero elsewhere

knowledge_statements.title: Closed Gauges with Nonclosed Infimal Convolution

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closure Repair by Closing the Generated Hull
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric lower-semicontinuous closure of a possibly nonclosed infimal gauge construction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C_i=\{x:\gamma_i(x)\leq1\}\) and \(D=\operatorname{conv}(C_1\cup C_2)\). Then \[\gamma_1\square\gamma_2=\gamma_D,\qquad \operatorname{cl}(\gamma_1\square\gamma_2)=\gamma_{\overline D}.\] Consequently, the infimal construction is lower semicontinuous exactly when \(\gamma_D=\gamma_{\overline D}\). Closedness of \(C_1\) and \(C_2\) separately does not guarantee this equality because their convex hull need not be closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closing an infimal gauge construction amounts to replacing the convex hull of its unit sets by its closure.
assumptions_latex: \(\gamma_1,\gamma_2\) are proper lower-semicontinuous gauges with unit sets \(C_1,C_2\).

notation.meaning: convex hull of the two unit sets
lower-semicontinuous hull of an extended-real convex function

review_flags: The equality concerns gauges and their lower-semicontinuous hulls; a nonclosed generator need not equal the unit sublevel set of its gauge.

children.title: Linear-Quotient Gauge Transport
children.top_down_role: Gauge transport through linear mappings.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Pullback and quotient transport of a gauge
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(A:E\to F\) be linear between finite-dimensional real vector spaces. Let \(\gamma:E\to[0,+\infty]\) and \(\eta:F\to[0,+\infty]\) be gauges.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Both contravariant pullback and covariant infimal transport are included. The quotient formula is extended-valued outside the range of the map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The pullback of \(\eta\) through \(A\) is \[A^*\eta:E\to[0,+\infty],\qquad (A^*\eta)(x)=\eta(Ax).\] The quotient or infimal image of \(\gamma\) through \(A\) is \[A_\#\gamma:F\to[0,+\infty],\qquad (A_\#\gamma)(y)=\inf\{\gamma(x):Ax=y\},\] with \(\inf\varnothing=+\infty\). Both are gauges. If \(C_\gamma=\{x:\gamma(x)\le1\}\) and \(C_\eta=\{y:\eta(y)\le1\}\), then \[C_{A^*\eta}=A^{-1}C_\eta,\qquad C_{A_\#\gamma}=A(C_\gamma)\] when the fiber infimum is attained; in general the closed quotient gauge has unit set \(\operatorname{cl}A(C_\gamma)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A gauge can be transported through a linear map in two directions. Pullback evaluates the target gauge after applying the map and has the inverse image of the target unit set as its unit set. Quotient transport minimizes the source gauge over the affine fiber mapping to a target point; it is infinite outside the range and has the image of the source unit set as its unit set when the minimum is attained. Closure may be needed because a linear image of a closed convex set need not be closed.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\operatorname{epi}(A^*\eta)\) is the inverse image of \(\operatorname{epi}\eta\) under \((x,t)\mapsto(Ax,t)\).
\(\operatorname{epi}(A_\#\gamma)\) is the lower boundary generated by the image of \(\operatorname{epi}\gamma\) under \((x,t)\mapsto(Ax,t)\).
special_cases_latex: If \(A\) is injective, pullback restricts a gauge to an embedded subspace.
If \(A\) is surjective, \(A_\#\gamma\) is the quotient gauge on \(F\cong E/\ker A\).
immediate_consequences_latex: \(\ker A\subseteq\{x:(A^*\eta)(x)=0\}\).
A polyhedral source gauge has a polyhedral quotient gauge, and its fiber infimum is attained whenever finite.
boundary_notes: Closedness of \(A_\#\gamma\) is not automatic for arbitrary closed nonpolyhedral gauges.
The notation \(A^*\eta\) here denotes functional pullback, not the adjoint-map action on dual vectors.

notation.meaning: Infimal or quotient image of gamma through A.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the pullback gauge \(r=p\circ A\), its zero set is exactly \[\{x\in X:r(x)=0\}=A^{-1}(Z_p).\] Since \(A x=0\) for every \(x\in\ker A\) and every gauge satisfies \(p(0)=0\), one always has \(\ker A\subseteq A^{-1}(Z_p)\). If \(p\) is definite, meaning \(Z_p=\{0\}\), then \(r(x)=0\) holds exactly when \(x\in\ker A\). Hence the pullback descends to a definite gauge on \(X/\ker A\).
