knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite Membership Access Cannot Give Exact Unrestricted Evaluation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Information boundary for exact recovery of unrestricted real gauge values from membership comparisons.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(x\ne0\). Over any admissible family for which \(\gamma_C(x)\) ranges through a nondegenerate real interval, no deterministic procedure using finitely many exact queries of the form \(x/t\in C\) can recover \(\gamma_C(x)\) exactly for every member of the family. Prescribed-accuracy evaluation remains possible through threshold search.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finitely many membership comparisons cannot identify an unrestricted real gauge value exactly, although they can approximate it to any positive tolerance.
assumptions_latex: The admissible gauge family permits \(\gamma_C(x)\) to range through a nondegenerate real interval.
Only finitely many exact membership queries are allowed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact finite-query evaluation is impossible without additional discreteness or algebraic structure.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Corrected Bisection Reduction from Membership to Gauge Evaluation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Prescribed-accuracy pointwise evaluation from exact scaled unit-ball membership, including the zero-query accuracy regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\gamma_C\) be a finite gauge with unit ball \(C=\{z:\gamma_C(z)\leq1\}\), fix \(x\), and suppose a known \(R>0\) satisfies \(\gamma_C(x)\leq R\). For every \(t>0\),
\[
x/t\in C\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\gamma_C(x)\leq t.
\]
If \(0<\varepsilon<R\), bisection of \([0,R]\) using these exact membership tests produces an interval containing \(\gamma_C(x)\) with width at most \(\varepsilon\) after at most \(\lceil\log_2(R/\varepsilon)\rceil\) queries. If \(\varepsilon\geq R\), no query is needed. Thus the universal bound is
\[
\max\{0,\lceil\log_2(R/\varepsilon)\rceil\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scaled exact membership gives gauge threshold comparisons, so bisection evaluates a bounded gauge value to absolute accuracy ε in max(0, ceiling(log₂(R/ε))) queries.
assumptions_latex: A query point \(x\) and a known bound \(R>0\) with \(\gamma_C(x)\leq R\) are given.
Exact membership queries for \(C\) are available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An interval of width at most \(\varepsilon\) containing \(\gamma_C(x)\) is obtained using at most \(\max\{0,\lceil\log_2(R/\varepsilon)\rceil\}\) membership queries.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle-information boundary for unrestricted real gauge values, distinct from approximate binary-search evaluation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(x\ne0\) and suppose only finitely many exact membership queries of the form \(x/t\in C\) are permitted. children.title: Polar-Gauge Support-Oracle Equivalence
children.top_down_role: Dual evaluation through support optimization.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex with \(0\in C\). Let \(\kappa_C=\gamma_C\), and define \(C^\circ=\{y:\langle y,x\rangle\le1\ \forall x\in C\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact finite-dimensional value-oracle equivalence; an optimizer-returning support oracle is stronger than a value-only polar-gauge oracle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The polar gauge of \(\kappa_C\) is the support function of its unit ball: \(\kappa_C^\circ(y)=\sigma_C(y)=\sup\{\langle y,x\rangle:x\in C\}\). Hence a value support oracle for \(C\) and a value evaluation oracle for \(\kappa_C^\circ\) are the same map. An optimizing support oracle additionally returns \(x_y\in C\) with \(\langle y,x_y\rangle=\kappa_C^\circ(y)\) when the supremum is finite and attained. Polar membership satisfies \(y\in sC^\circ\iff\kappa_C^\circ(y)\le s\) for \(s\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The polar gauge evaluated at a dual vector equals the support value of the primal gauge unit ball in that direction. Therefore a support-value oracle for the unit ball is exactly a polar-gauge value oracle. An oracle that also returns a maximizing point contains additional information and requires attainment. Membership in a scaled polar ball is equivalent to comparing the support value with the scale.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(C^\circ=\{y:\sigma_C(y)\le1\}=\{y:\kappa_C^\circ(y)\le1\}.\)
special_cases_latex: For a balanced norm ball, the identity is the usual dual-norm support formula.
immediate_consequences_latex: A returned support maximizer is an exposed point or belongs to the exposed face selected by \(y\).
boundary_notes: If \(C\) is unbounded, the support value may be \(+\infty\).
A finite supremum need not be attained when compactness is absent.
Approximate support and approximate polar evaluation require matched additive or relative error conventions.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\) be a nonempty closed bounded convex subset of a Banach space \(X\). Then \(K\) is weakly compact if and only if every \(y\in X^*\) attains its support value on \(K\): \[\forall y\in X^*\;\exists x_y\in K:\quad \langle y,x_y\rangle=\sigma_K(y).\] In particular, compact sets in finite-dimensional spaces admit exact support points in every direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: James's theorem characterizes weak compactness of a closed bounded convex set by attainment of every continuous linear functional; finite-dimensional compactness is the standard specialization.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subset X\) is nonempty, closed, bounded, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: K\text{ is weakly compact}\iff\forall y\in X^*,\;\sigma_K(y)\text{ is attained on }K.

notation.meaning: Continuous dual of the Banach space.

knowledge_statements.title: James Weak-Compactness Characterization

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard sufficient condition for exact support-point output in locally convex spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\) be a nonempty weakly compact subset of a Banach space \(X\). For every \(y\in X^*\), the map \(x\mapsto\langle y,x\rangle\) is weakly continuous and therefore attains its maximum on \(K\): \[\sigma_K(y)=\max_{x\in K}\langle y,x\rangle.\] Consequently, compactness in finite dimensions, and weak compactness in infinite dimensions, suffice for an exact support-point oracle in every direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every continuous linear functional attains its support value on a nonempty weakly compact set; finite-dimensional compactness is the usual special case.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subset X\) is nonempty and weakly compact.

notation.meaning: Continuous dual of the Banach space.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Feasibility Oracle for an Antipolar Region
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and closed with \(0\notin C\). Define its antipolar by \(C'=\{y:\langle y,x\rangle\ge1\ \forall x\in C\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact finite-dimensional feasibility access for reverse-separation regions used in gauge duality; approximate variants require a declared margin.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An antipolar feasibility oracle for \(C\) is a predicate \(\mathrm{Feas}_{C'}(y)\) satisfying \(\mathrm{Feas}_{C'}(y)=1\iff y\in C'\iff\inf_{x\in C}\langle y,x\rangle\ge1\). A certifying oracle may, upon rejection, return \(x_y\in C\) with \(\langle y,x_y\rangle<1\); upon acceptance it certifies the universal lower bound. For a scaled threshold \(\alpha>0\), the region \(C'_\alpha=\{y:\langle y,x\rangle\ge\alpha\ \forall x\in C\}\) obeys \(C'_\alpha=\alpha C'\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The antipolar of a set not containing the origin consists of dual vectors whose pairing with every primal feasible point is at least one. An exact feasibility oracle accepts precisely those vectors. Equivalently, it checks whether the infimum of the linear functional over the primal set is at least one. A certifying rejection oracle supplies a primal point violating that inequality. Positive threshold changes correspond to scaling the antipolar region.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Rejection has a finite witness when there exists \(x_y\in C\) satisfying \(\langle y,x_y\rangle<1\).
special_cases_latex: If \(C=\{x:Ax=b\}\) intersects an appropriate gauge domain, the oracle tests the reverse-separation constraints appearing in gauge-dual feasible regions.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every accepted vector strictly separates the origin from \(C\) at normalized margin one.
boundary_notes: If \(0\in C\), then \(C'\) is empty.
For nonclosed or unbounded sets, the infimum may be unattained, so rejection need not have an optimizing witness.
An approximate oracle must distinguish acceptance, rejection, and an uncertainty band around level one.

notation.meaning: Antipolar or reverse-polar set of the primal region.

assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a nonempty closed convex subset of a real Hilbert space and \(0\notin C\).
\(C'=\{y:\langle y,x\rangle\geq1\text{ for all }x\in C\}\) is its antipolar.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For each query \(z\), the oracle either confirms \(z\in C'\) or returns a halfspace containing \(C'\) and excluding \(z\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On input \(z\), an antipolar separation oracle first tests whether \(\inf_{x\in C}\langle z,x\rangle\geq1\). If so, it returns feasible. Otherwise it returns \(a\neq0\) and \(\beta\) such that \[\langle a,z\rangle<\beta\leq\langle a,y\rangle\quad\text{for every }y\in C'.\] Thus the reported closed halfspace contains the entire antipolar while excluding the query. The definition requires a strong separating pair, not merely a declaration of infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The oracle recognizes antipolar membership or supplies a valid halfspace containing the antipolar and strictly excluding the query.

children.title: Antipolar Projection Oracles
children.top_down_role: Feasibility access through nearest-point computations for antipolar regions.

assumptions_latex: \(C'\) is a nonempty closed convex antipolar subset of a real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The oracle returns the unique \(p=P_{C'}z\) and the inequality \(\langle z-p,y-p\rangle\leq0\) for every \(y\in C'\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact metric-projection oracle and its induced separation certificate.

source_refs.locator: 3.4 Separation p. 64

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(z\), the oracle returns \[p=P_{C'}z=\mathop{\operatorname{argmin}}_{y\in C'}\tfrac12\|y-z\|^2.\] Closedness and convexity make \(p\) unique. Its optimality condition is \(\langle z-p,y-p\rangle\leq0\) for all \(y\in C'\). If \(z\notin C'\), then \(p\neq z\), and this inequality defines a separating halfspace containing \(C'\); if \(p=z\), the oracle certifies membership.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The projection oracle returns the nearest antipolar point; its variational inequality also yields membership or separation.
knowledge_statements.title: Antipolar Projection Oracles

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact projection onto a nonempty closed convex antipolar is firmly nonexpansive and therefore 1-Lipschitz in the query.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A vector \(y\) with \(\inf_{x\in C}\langle y,x\rangle\geq1\) is a directly verifiable certificate that \(C'\neq\varnothing\). Conversely, a point certificate \(0\in C\) proves \(C'=\varnothing\), since it would require \(0=\langle y,0\rangle\geq1\). If \(0\notin C\), strong separation supplies \(u\) and \(\alpha>0\) with \(\inf_{x\in C}\langle u,x\rangle\geq\alpha\); then \(u/\alpha\in C'\). Hence these alternatives are exhaustive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Antipolar nonemptiness is certified by a feasible dual vector; membership of zero in the original closed convex set certifies emptiness.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Computational Tractability Boundary for Gauge Models
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\{C_I\}\) be a family of finite-dimensional gauge unit sets indexed by finite encodings \(I\), with gauges \(\kappa_I\) and polars \(C_I^\circ\). Fix a computational model, query domain, norm, and accuracy convention.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complexity classification of represented or oracle-accessed gauge families; the definition is relative rather than an intrinsic property of an abstract convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A tractability boundary for \(\{C_I\}\) is a stated partition of access tasks and parameter regimes into those admitting algorithms polynomial in \(|I|\) and the declared accuracy size, and those for which such access is unavailable or complexity-hard under a specified reduction. Relevant tasks include exact or weak membership in \(C_I\), evaluation of \(\kappa_I\), separation, support optimization, evaluation of \(\kappa_I^\circ\), and construction of certificates. A boundary statement is well-formed only when it specifies the representation, task, approximation metric, conditioning or radius promises, and complexity assumption.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A gauge tractability boundary identifies where a family of gauge computations changes from efficiently accessible to unavailable or complexity-hard. The classification is always tied to an input representation, a particular task, an approximation convention, geometric promises, and a computational model. Evaluation, membership, separation, support optimization, polar evaluation, and certificate construction are distinct tasks and can lie on different sides of the boundary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal T=\{(I,\mathrm{task},\varepsilon,\mathrm{promises}):\mathrm{task}(C_I)\text{ is solvable within the declared polynomial resource bound}\}\) defines the tractable side only relative to the declared access model.
special_cases_latex: A gauge may have easy evaluation but a difficult proximal map.
An atomic hull may have an easy atom-membership test but a hard support-optimization problem.
immediate_consequences_latex: A complexity claim about one representation cannot automatically be transferred to a more succinct representation of the same abstract set.
boundary_notes: Exact and approximate tractability are different classifications.
Poor conditioning can prevent polynomial oracle reductions even when formal convex-analytic identities hold.
Hardness must name its reduction and complexity assumption; lack of a known algorithm is not hardness.

notation.meaning: Encoded input length of the gauge instance.
Declared tractable region of instances and access tasks.

children.title: Intractable Atomic Hulls
children.top_down_role: Atomic gauges lacking practical exact representations or support oracles.

assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is an atomic family and \(K=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(\mathcal A\cup\{0\})\).
Exact linear optimization \(\sup_{a\in\mathcal A}\langle y,a\rangle\) is computationally intractable for the represented family.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact evaluation of \(\sigma_K(y)\), and hence of \(\gamma_{K^\circ}(y)\), inherits the same optimization obstruction.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional tractability boundary linking atomic linear optimization, support evaluation, and polar-gauge evaluation.

source_refs.locator: 7.2 Support Functions p. 135; 7.3 Polar Sets p. 136

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every query \(y\), linearity and closure give \[\sigma_K(y)=\sup_{a\in\mathcal A\cup\{0\}}\langle y,a\rangle=\max\left\{0,\sup_{a\in\mathcal A}\langle y,a\rangle\right\}.\] Polarity then yields \(\gamma_{K^\circ}(y)=\sigma_K(y)\). Thus an atomic description is not by itself a tractable representation: whenever exact linear optimization over the represented atom family lacks a practical oracle, exact support and polar-gauge evaluation inherit that obstruction. A family-specific complexity classification requires an explicit encoding and computational model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An atomic hull is not automatically tractable: hard linear optimization over its atoms makes exact support and polar-gauge evaluation hard as well.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: For every finite encoding \(I\), let \(\mathcal A_I\subset\mathbb{Q}^{n(I)}\) be a succinctly represented atomic family, let \(C_I=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(\mathcal A_I\cup\{0\})\), and let \(\gamma_I=\gamma_{C_I}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case complexity of families of rationally encoded atomic hulls; intractability is task- and approximation-specific rather than a property of one unencoded set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The family \(\{C_I\}\) is an intractable atomic-hull family for a declared task if that task is hard under a specified polynomial-time reduction and complexity assumption. Canonical tasks are weak membership in \(C_I\), evaluation or approximation of \(\gamma_I(x)\), and support optimization \(\sigma_{C_I}(y)=\sup_{a\in\mathcal A_I}\langle y,a\rangle\). For approximate hardness, the encoding must specify a rational tolerance \(\varepsilon\), bounded query data, and a promised gap between accepted and rejected cases. Intractability of support immediately concerns polar-gauge evaluation because \(\gamma_I^\circ=\sigma_{C_I}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An intractable atomic hull is defined as a family, not merely as a complicated-looking convex set. Each instance has a succinct atomic description, and the hull is the closed convex hull of the atoms and the origin. The family is intractable only for a named computational task, approximation gap, reduction, and complexity assumption. Typical tasks are weak membership, atomic-gauge evaluation, and support optimization. Support hardness is also polar-gauge evaluation hardness because those values coincide.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_I=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(\mathcal A_I\cup\{0\}),\quad \gamma_I(x)=\inf\{t\ge0:x\in tC_I\},\quad \gamma_I^\circ(y)=\sup_{a\in\mathcal A_I}\langle y,a\rangle,\) with intractability attached to a precisely declared one of these computational tasks.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Support optimization over \(C_I\) and over \(\mathcal A_I\) have the same optimal value.
special_cases_latex: If linear optimization over \(\mathcal A_I\) encodes a known hard combinatorial optimization problem, exact polar-gauge evaluation inherits that declared hardness under the corresponding reduction.
immediate_consequences_latex: A polynomial-size listing of all atoms can remove succinct-representation hardness even when the same abstract construction has exponentially many atoms under another encoding.
boundary_notes: A hard exact task may admit a polynomial-time approximation scheme or relaxation.
Atom-membership hardness, hull-membership hardness, and support hardness are distinct claims.
No hardness conclusion is valid without a specified reduction, encoding, and complexity assumption.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Inner-Outer Gauge Approximation Pair and Its Distortion
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathbb E\) be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space. A convex body used as a gauge unit set is a closed convex set \(C\subset\mathbb E\) with \(0\in\operatorname{int}C\). Its gauge is \(\gamma_C(x):=\inf\{t>0:x\in tC\}\). Its polar is \(C^\circ:=\{y\in\mathbb E:\langle y,x\rangle\leq 1\text{ for every }x\in C\}\), and its support function is \(\sigma_C(y):=\sup_{x\in C}\langle y,x\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This definition concerns finite-dimensional, exact set inclusions and multiplicative representation quality. The sets need not be symmetric, so their gauges need not be norms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An inner-outer gauge approximation pair for \(C\) is an ordered pair \((C_{\mathrm{in}},C_{\mathrm{out}})\) of closed convex sets satisfying \(0\in\operatorname{int}C_{\mathrm{in}}\) and \[C_{\mathrm{in}}\subseteq C\subseteq C_{\mathrm{out}}.\] The pair has multiplicative distortion at most \(\eta\geq1\) when, in addition, \[C_{\mathrm{out}}\subseteq \eta C_{\mathrm{in}}.\] Its associated lower and upper gauge models are respectively \(\gamma_{C_{\mathrm{out}}}\) and \(\gamma_{C_{\mathrm{in}}}\); for every \(x\in\mathbb E\), they satisfy \[\gamma_{C_{\mathrm{out}}}(x)\leq\gamma_C(x)\leq\gamma_{C_{\mathrm{in}}}(x)\leq\eta\gamma_{C_{\mathrm{out}}}(x).\] Equivalently, the polar bodies obey \[(C_{\mathrm{out}})^\circ\subseteq C^\circ\subseteq(C_{\mathrm{in}})^\circ\subseteq\eta(C_{\mathrm{out}})^\circ.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a closed convex gauge unit set \(C\) containing the origin in its interior, an inner-outer approximation pair consists of closed convex sets \(C_{\mathrm{in}}\) and \(C_{\mathrm{out}}\) with \(C_{\mathrm{in}}\subseteq C\subseteq C_{\mathrm{out}}\). It has distortion at most \(\eta\) if \(C_{\mathrm{out}}\subseteq\eta C_{\mathrm{in}}\). The outer set supplies a lower bound on the true gauge, the inner set supplies an upper bound, and their ratio is bounded by \(\eta\). Polarity reverses the three inclusions and gives the equivalent polar approximation.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathbb E\) is finite-dimensional and carries a fixed inner product.
\(0\in\operatorname{int}C_{\mathrm{in}}\), hence all three gauges are finite on \(\mathbb E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[(C_{\mathrm{in}},C_{\mathrm{out}})\text{ is an }\eta\text{-inner-outer gauge approximation pair}\iff C_{\mathrm{in}}\subseteq C\subseteq C_{\mathrm{out}}\subseteq\eta C_{\mathrm{in}}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The set inclusions are equivalent to \[\gamma_{C_{\mathrm{out}}}\leq\gamma_C\leq\gamma_{C_{\mathrm{in}}}\leq\eta\gamma_{C_{\mathrm{out}}}\quad\text{pointwise on }\mathbb E.\]

Using \(\gamma_D=\sigma_{D^\circ}\), the same approximation is represented by \[\sigma_{(C_{\mathrm{out}})^\circ}\leq\sigma_{C^\circ}\leq\sigma_{(C_{\mathrm{in}})^\circ}\leq\eta\sigma_{(C_{\mathrm{out}})^\circ}.\]
special_cases_latex: If \(\eta=1\), then \(C_{\mathrm{in}}=C=C_{\mathrm{out}}\), so both models equal the exact gauge.
If all three sets are centrally symmetric, their gauges are norms and the definition becomes a multiplicative norm approximation.
immediate_consequences_latex: If \(\gamma_{C_{\mathrm{in}}}(x)\leq1\), then \(x\in C_{\mathrm{in}}\subseteq C\). If \(\gamma_{C_{\mathrm{out}}}(x)>1\), then \(x\notin C_{\mathrm{out}}\), hence \(x\notin C\).
For every nonzero \(x\), \[1\leq\frac{\gamma_{C_{\mathrm{in}}}(x)}{\gamma_{C_{\mathrm{out}}}(x)}\leq\eta.\]
boundary_notes: If the origin is not interior to the inner set, the gauges may take the value \(+\infty\), and a finite global distortion factor need not exist.
The term “inner-outer” here denotes simultaneous set containment, not Painlevé-Kuratowski inner and outer limits.
Membership is not decided when \(\gamma_{C_{\mathrm{out}}}(x)\leq1<\gamma_{C_{\mathrm{in}}}(x)\); this is the approximation band.

children.title: Inner Gauge Approximations
children.top_down_role: Approximate gauge models based on inner geometric containment.

assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is closed, convex, absorbing, and contains \(0\).
\(K_{\mathrm{in}}\subseteq K\) is closed, convex, absorbing, and contains \(0\).

notation.meaning: Inner approximation of the unit ball.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inner approximation refers to containment of unit balls and therefore gives an upper gauge bound.

source_refs.locator: 7 Support Functions and Polar Sets p. 133

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An inner gauge approximation of \(K\) is the gauge generated by an approximating unit ball \(K_{\mathrm{in}}\subseteq K\): \[\gamma_{K_{\mathrm{in}}}(x)=\inf\{t>0:x\in tK_{\mathrm{in}}\}.\] Since \(tK_{\mathrm{in}}\subseteq tK\) for every \(t>0\), any scale feasible for \(K_{\mathrm{in}}\) is feasible for \(K\). Consequently \(\gamma_K(x)\leq\gamma_{K_{\mathrm{in}}}(x)\) for all \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smaller approximating unit ball produces a larger gauge, so an inner unit-ball approximation is an upper approximation of gauge values.
knowledge_statements.title: Inner Gauge Approximations

children.title: Outer Gauge Approximations
children.top_down_role: Approximate gauge models based on outer geometric containment.

assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is closed, convex, absorbing, and contains \(0\).
\(K\subseteq K_{\mathrm{out}}\) and \(K_{\mathrm{out}}\) is closed, convex, absorbing, and contains \(0\).

notation.meaning: Outer approximation of the unit ball.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Outer approximation refers to containment of unit balls and therefore gives a lower gauge bound.

source_refs.locator: 7 Support Functions and Polar Sets p. 133

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An outer gauge approximation of \(K\) is the gauge generated by an approximating unit ball \(K\subseteq K_{\mathrm{out}}\): \[\gamma_{K_{\mathrm{out}}}(x)=\inf\{t>0:x\in tK_{\mathrm{out}}\}.\] Since \(tK\subseteq tK_{\mathrm{out}}\) for every \(t>0\), every scale feasible for \(K\) is feasible for \(K_{\mathrm{out}}\). Consequently \(\gamma_{K_{\mathrm{out}}}(x)\leq\gamma_K(x)\) for all \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A larger approximating unit ball produces a smaller gauge, so an outer unit-ball approximation is a lower approximation of gauge values.

children.title: Approximation Ordering
children.top_down_role: Containment-based comparison of approximate gauge models.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
\(K_{\mathrm{in}},K,K_{\mathrm{out}}\subset X\) are closed convex sets containing \(0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-inclusion ordering for inner and outer gauge approximations.

source_refs.locator: 7.2 Support Functions p. 135; 7.3 Polar Sets p. 136

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(K_{\mathrm{in}}\subseteq K\subseteq K_{\mathrm{out}}\), then inclusion reverses the corresponding gauges: \[\gamma_{K_{\mathrm{out}}}(x)\leq\gamma_K(x)\leq\gamma_{K_{\mathrm{in}}}(x)\qquad(x\in X).\] Polarity reverses inclusion, whereas support functions preserve it: \[K_{\mathrm{out}}^{\circ}\subseteq K^{\circ}\subseteq K_{\mathrm{in}}^{\circ},\qquad \sigma_{K_{\mathrm{in}}}(y)\leq\sigma_K(y)\leq\sigma_{K_{\mathrm{out}}}(y)\qquad(y\in X).\] These conclusions remain valid with extended-valued gauges when the sets are not absorbing.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inner-outer set sandwich gives reverse gauge bounds, reverse polar inclusions, and forward support-function bounds.
knowledge_statements.title: Approximation Ordering

children.top_down_role: Tradeoffs between approximation fidelity and representation complexity.

assumptions_latex: All sets are closed, convex, and contain \(0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiplicative quality guarantee for a tractable inner-outer representation pair.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a computationally tractable pair satisfies \(K_{\mathrm{in}}\subseteq K\subseteq K_{\mathrm{out}}\subseteq\alpha K_{\mathrm{in}}\). Positive homogeneity and inclusion monotonicity give \[\alpha^{-1}\gamma_{K_{\mathrm{in}}}(x)\leq\gamma_{K_{\mathrm{out}}}(x)\leq\gamma_K(x)\leq\gamma_{K_{\mathrm{in}}}(x)\qquad(x\in X).\] Equivalently, the polar sandwich is \[\alpha^{-1}K_{\mathrm{in}}^{\circ}\subseteq K_{\mathrm{out}}^{\circ}\subseteq K^{\circ}\subseteq K_{\mathrm{in}}^{\circ}.\] Thus the representation factor \(\alpha\) directly bounds the worst-case multiplicative loss in gauge value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the outer model lies within an alpha-scaling of the inner model, their computable gauges approximate the true gauge within the same factor.
knowledge_statements.title: Representation-Quality Tradeoffs

children.title: Ill-Conditioned Polar Geometry
children.top_down_role: Sensitivity and numerical instability associated with narrow or nearly degenerate polar regions.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is Euclidean with closed unit ball \(B\).
\(K\subset X\) is closed and convex with \(rB\subseteq K\subseteq RB\), where \(0<r\leq R<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditioning boundary determined by inner and outer radii around the origin.

source_refs.locator: 7 Support Functions and Polar Sets p. 133; 7.3 Polar Sets p. 136
source_refs.source_title: Convex Analysis and Monotone Operator Theory in Hilbert Spaces

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Polarity transforms the radial sandwich into \[R^{-1}B\subseteq K^{\circ}\subseteq r^{-1}B.\] Moreover, for all \(x,z\in X\), \[\left|\gamma_K(x)-\gamma_K(z)\right|\leq r^{-1}\lVert x-z\rVert.\] Hence the ratio \(\kappa=R/r\) measures radial ill-conditioning, while the absolute sensitivity of gauge evaluation is controlled by \(r^{-1}\). As \(r\downarrow0\), these uniform bounds diverge; at \(r=0\), the gauge may cease to be finite or locally Lipschitz on all of \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A small inner radius produces a large polar radius and unstable gauge evaluation; when the inner radius vanishes, global finiteness and Lipschitz control may fail.
knowledge_statements.title: Ill-Conditioned Polar Geometry

source_witnesses.locator: 7 Support Functions and Polar Sets p. 133; 7.3 Polar Sets p. 136
source_witnesses.source_title: Convex Analysis and Monotone Operator Theory in Hilbert Spaces

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A rectangular family showing sharp gauge sensitivity and loss of finiteness at degeneration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(0<r\le1\), let \(K_r=[-r,r]\times[-1,1]\subset\mathbb R^2\). Then \[\gamma_{K_r}(x)=\max\{|x_1|/r,|x_2|\},\qquad K_r^\circ=\{y:r|y_1|+|y_2|\le1\}.\] The Euclidean Lipschitz modulus of \(\gamma_{K_r}\) is \(1/r\), and the polar reaches distance \(1/r\) along the first coordinate. At \(r=0\), \(K_0=\{0\}\times[-1,1]\) and \(\gamma_{K_0}(x)=+\infty\) whenever \(x_1\ne0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Thin rectangles attain the inverse-inner-radius sensitivity scale, while the degenerate limit has an infinite gauge outside its span.
assumptions_latex: \(0<r\le1\) for the nondegenerate family; \(r=0\) for its limiting set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The sensitivity and polar radius grow as \(1/r\), and global gauge finiteness fails at \(r=0\).

notation.meaning: polar of the rectangular gauge ball

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polar Asphericity and Geometric Condition Number
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathbb E\) be a finite-dimensional normed space with unit ball \(B:=\{x:\|x\|\leq1\}\), dual norm \(\|\cdot\|_*\), and dual unit ball \(B_*\). Let \(C\subset\mathbb E\) be closed and convex with \(0\in\operatorname{int}C\), and put \(P:=C^\circ\). When \(C\) is also bounded, \(P\) is a compact convex body containing the origin in its interior.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The condition number is relative to a specified reference norm. It measures finite-dimensional global radial asphericity of the polar body, not local boundary curvature or floating-point conditioning of a particular algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the polar inradius and outradius relative to \(B_*\) by \[r_*(P):=\sup\{r>0:rB_*\subseteq P\},\qquad R_*(P):=\inf\{R>0:P\subseteq RB_*\}.\] The polar geometric condition number and asphericity coefficient are \[\kappa_*(P):=\frac{R_*(P)}{r_*(P)},\qquad \alpha_*(P):=\frac{r_*(P)}{R_*(P)}=\kappa_*(P)^{-1}.\] For a prescribed level \(K>1\), the polar geometry is called \(K\)-ill-conditioned when \(\kappa_*(P)\geq K\), equivalently \(\alpha_*(P)\leq K^{-1}\). It is degenerate when \(r_*(P)=0\) or \(R_*(P)=+\infty\), in which case \(\kappa_*(P):=+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The conditioning of a polar body \(P=C^\circ\) is measured by comparing its largest contained dual-norm ball with its smallest containing dual-norm ball. Their radii are \(r_*(P)\) and \(R_*(P)\), and the ratio \(R_*(P)/r_*(P)\) is the polar geometric condition number. Geometry is ill-conditioned at level \(K\) when this ratio is at least \(K\). A vanishing inradius or infinite outradius is declared degenerate and has infinite condition number.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathbb E\) is finite-dimensional and \(\|\cdot\|\) is a fixed reference norm.
\(C\subset\mathbb E\) is closed and convex with \(0\in\operatorname{int}C\), and \(P=C^\circ\).
For finite conditioning, \(C\) is bounded, equivalently \(0\in\operatorname{int}P\), so \(0<r_*(P)\leq R_*(P)<+\infty\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: Because \(\gamma_C=\sigma_{C^\circ}=\sigma_P\), \[r_*(P)=\min_{\|x\|=1}\gamma_C(x),\qquad R_*(P)=\max_{\|x\|=1}\gamma_C(x),\] and therefore \[\kappa_*(P)=\frac{\max_{\|x\|=1}\gamma_C(x)}{\min_{\|x\|=1}\gamma_C(x)}.\]
The radius sandwich \(r_*B_*\subseteq P\subseteq R_*B_*\) is equivalent by polarity to \[R_*^{-1}B\subseteq C\subseteq r_*^{-1}B.\]
special_cases_latex: For an ellipsoid \(P=\{y:\langle Hy,y\rangle\leq1\}\) measured in the Euclidean norm, \(\kappa_*(P)=\sqrt{\lambda_{\max}(H)/\lambda_{\min}(H)}\).
If \(P\) is a positive scalar multiple of \(B_*\), then \(r_*(P)=R_*(P)\) and \(\kappa_*(P)=1\).
immediate_consequences_latex: For every \(x\in\mathbb E\), \[r_*(P)\|x\|\leq\gamma_C(x)\leq R_*(P)\|x\|.\]
After normalizing \(R_*(P)=1\), increasing ill-conditioning is exactly the narrowing regime \(r_*(P)\downarrow0\).
The number \(\kappa_*(P)\) is invariant under positive rescaling of \(P\).
boundary_notes: The numerical value depends on the reference norm; a coordinate change must transform both the body and the norm to preserve it.
A large condition number records global anisotropy but does not by itself identify a nonsmooth point, a small curvature radius, or a particular unstable algorithm.
If \(C\) is unbounded, its polar may have empty interior and the finite-radius definition enters the degenerate case.

notation.meaning: Polar body whose geometry is being conditioned.
Largest radius of a centered dual-norm ball contained in \(P\).
Smallest radius of a centered dual-norm ball containing \(P\).
Polar condition number and reciprocal asphericity coefficient.

children.title: Inexact Oracle-Certificate Reliability Boundary
children.top_down_role: Reliability limits under approximate gauge, support, or antipolar computations.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Reliability Boundary for an Interval-Certified Inexact Oracle
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(q\in\mathbb R\) be an exact scalar gauge value, support value, polar residual, or other scalar certificate quantity, and let the exact decision predicate be \(q\leq\tau\) for a fixed threshold \(\tau\in\mathbb R\). An inexact oracle reports \(\widehat q\in\mathbb R\) together with certified one-sided errors \(\varepsilon_-,\varepsilon_+\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This definition treats deterministic, certified scalar error bounds. It does not cover merely heuristic error estimates, stochastic confidence intervals, vector-valued separation errors, or unbounded oracle outputs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The oracle enclosure is \[I(\widehat q):=[L,U]:=[\widehat q-\varepsilon_-,\widehat q+\varepsilon_+],\qquad L\leq q\leq U.\] The report is a reliable positive certificate for \(q\leq\tau\) when \(U\leq\tau\), and a reliable negative certificate when \(L>\tau\). Its reliability boundary, or unresolved band, is \[\mathcal B_\tau:=\{(\widehat q,\varepsilon_-,\varepsilon_+):\widehat q-\varepsilon_-\leq\tau<\widehat q+\varepsilon_+\}.\] Thus a report belongs to \(\mathcal B_\tau\) exactly when its certified interval contains values on both sides of the decision boundary, with equality assigned to the predicate \(q\leq\tau\). No truth value for that predicate is certified by such a report.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inexact oracle is reliable only through its certified interval from \(L=\widehat q-\varepsilon_-\) to \(U=\widehat q+\varepsilon_+\). It certifies \(q\leq\tau\) if the entire interval lies at or below \(\tau\), and certifies the opposite if the entire interval lies strictly above \(\tau\). The reliability boundary consists of all reports whose interval straddles \(\tau\); those reports do not determine which exact decision is true.
assumptions_latex: The error bounds are valid: \(\widehat q-\varepsilon_-\leq q\leq\widehat q+\varepsilon_+\).
The certificate predicate and its equality convention are fixed as \(q\leq\tau\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[U\leq\tau\Rightarrow q\leq\tau,\qquad L>\tau\Rightarrow q>\tau,\qquad L\leq\tau<U\Rightarrow\text{the oracle report is unresolved}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The report is reliable precisely when \(I(\widehat q)\subseteq(-\infty,\tau]\) or \(I(\widehat q)\subseteq(\tau,+\infty)\); otherwise it lies in \(\mathcal B_\tau\).
For symmetric error \(\varepsilon_- =\varepsilon_+=\varepsilon\), the unresolved condition is \[|\widehat q-\tau|\leq\varepsilon\] with the upper endpoint convention inherited from \(q\leq\tau\).
special_cases_latex: For gauge membership, take \(q=\gamma_C(x)\) and \(\tau=1\). Then \(U\leq1\) certifies \(x\in C\), whereas \(L>1\) certifies \(x\notin C\).
For a support inequality, take \(q=\sigma_C(y)\). Then \(U\leq\tau\) certifies \(\langle y,x\rangle\leq\tau\) for every \(x\in C\).
For an exact oracle, \(\varepsilon_- =\varepsilon_+=0\), so the unresolved band collapses to the threshold itself.
immediate_consequences_latex: A smaller error interval can convert an unresolved report into a certificate, but enlarging the interval cannot convert an unresolved report into a reliable one without changing its center.

If the exact margin is \(m:=|q-\tau|>0\) and a symmetric oracle satisfies \(|\widehat q-q|\leq\varepsilon<m/2\), then its certified interval of radius \(\varepsilon\) lies wholly on the correct side of \(\tau\).
An approximate numerical value without a valid enclosure supplies no certificate under this definition.
boundary_notes: The supplied sources support exact gauge membership and exact gap certificates but do not directly name or formalize this interval-based “reliability boundary.”
For a strict predicate such as \(q<\tau\), endpoint assignments and hence \(\mathcal B_\tau\) must be changed.
Multiplicative errors require positivity assumptions and should first be converted into a valid interval enclosure.
Antipolar conventions differ across formulations; the scalar quantity and comparison direction must be fixed before applying this definition.

notation.meaning: Exact certificate quantity and its reported approximation.
Certified lower and upper bounds on \(q\).

review_flags: No inspected source states the exact named definition with certified one-sided oracle errors and the boundary set \(\mathcal B_\tau\).
A direct source on inexact gauge, support, or antipolar oracle certificates is required before candidate promotion.
The formulation is a mathematically consistent synthesis rather than a source-verified canonical term.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An absolute-error \(\varepsilon\)-inexact gauge oracle for \(K\) maps each query \(x\in X\) to numbers \(\underline g(x),\overline g(x)\in\mathbb R\) satisfying \[\underline g(x)\leq\gamma_K(x)\leq\overline g(x),\qquad 0\leq\overline g(x)-\underline g(x)\leq\varepsilon.\] A one-sided implementation may return only a lower or upper bound, but then it cannot support certification requiring the missing inequality. The exact gauge oracle is recovered when \(\varepsilon=0\) and the two outputs coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inexact gauge oracle returns a certified interval containing the gauge value, with width no greater than its declared tolerance.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An absolute-error \(\varepsilon\)-inexact support oracle for \(C\) maps every direction \(y\in X\) to numbers \(\underline s(y),\overline s(y)\in\mathbb R\) such that \[\underline s(y)\leq\sigma_C(y):=\max_{x\in C}\langle y,x\rangle\leq\overline s(y),\qquad \overline s(y)-\underline s(y)\leq\varepsilon.\] If the oracle also returns \(x_{\varepsilon}\in C\) with \(\langle y,x_{\varepsilon}\rangle\geq\sigma_C(y)-\varepsilon\), then \(\langle y,x_{\varepsilon}\rangle\) is a valid lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inexact support oracle brackets the maximum linear value and may return a feasible point attaining that value within the declared tolerance.

children.title: Inexact Antipolar Oracles
children.top_down_role: Reliability limits for approximate antipolar feasibility access.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The oracle encloses \(m_C(y)\), whose threshold at \(1\) determines membership in \(C'\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(m_C(y):=\min_{x\in C}\langle y,x\rangle\), so that \(y\in C'\) exactly when \(m_C(y)\geq1\). An absolute-error \(\varepsilon\)-inexact antipolar oracle returns \(\underline m(y),\overline m(y)\in\mathbb R\) satisfying \[\underline m(y)\leq m_C(y)\leq\overline m(y),\qquad \overline m(y)-\underline m(y)\leq\varepsilon.\] Consequently, \(\underline m(y)\geq1\) certifies antipolar membership, while \(\overline m(y)<1\) certifies nonmembership; neither conclusion follows when the interval crosses \(1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inexact antipolar oracle brackets the minimum pairing; only intervals lying wholly above or below one decide antipolar membership.

children.title: Certificate Reliability Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Accuracy regimes where oracle-derived certificates become inconclusive.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
\(K\subset X\) is closed, convex, absorbing, and contains \(0\); \(C\subset X\) is nonempty and compact.
Every oracle interval is rigorous: it contains the corresponding exact scalar value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Gauge or polar membership is inconclusive from an interval alone exactly in the crossing case \(L\leq 1<U\), whereas antipolar membership is inconclusive from an interval alone exactly in the crossing case \(L<1\leq U\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp threshold rules for certificates derived solely from rigorous inexact-oracle intervals.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \([L_g,U_g]\), \([L_s,U_s]\), and \([L_m,U_m]\) contain, respectively, \(\gamma_K(x)\), \(\sigma_K(y)\), and \(m_C(y):=\min_{z\in C}\langle y,z\rangle\). For gauge feasibility \(\gamma_K(x)\leq1\), the condition \(U_g\leq1\) certifies membership and \(L_g>1\) certifies nonmembership. For polar membership \(y\in K^{\circ}\), equivalently \(\sigma_K(y)\leq1\), the condition \(U_s\leq1\) certifies membership and \(L_s>1\) certifies nonmembership. For antipolar membership \(y\in C'\), equivalently \(m_C(y)\geq1\), the condition \(L_m\geq1\) certifies membership and \(U_m<1\) certifies nonmembership. Using only the interval information, the respective inconclusive cases are \(L_g\leq1<U_g\), \(L_s\leq1<U_s\), and \(L_m<1\leq U_m\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rigorous interval certifies gauge or polar membership when its upper endpoint is at most one and antipolar membership when its lower endpoint is at least one. The inconclusive crossing condition includes equality on different endpoints for the two threshold directions.
knowledge_statements.title: Certificate Reliability Boundaries

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
\(K\subset X\) is closed, convex, absorbing, and contains \(0\); \(C\subset X\) is nonempty and compact.
Every oracle interval is rigorous: it contains the corresponding exact scalar value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Gauge or polar membership is inconclusive from an interval alone exactly in the crossing case \(L\leq 1<U\), whereas antipolar membership is inconclusive from an interval alone exactly in the crossing case \(L<1\leq U\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp threshold rules for certificates derived solely from rigorous inexact-oracle intervals.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \([L_g,U_g]\), \([L_s,U_s]\), and \([L_m,U_m]\) contain, respectively, \(\gamma_K(x)\), \(\sigma_K(y)\), and \(m_C(y):=\min_{z\in C}\langle y,z\rangle\). For gauge feasibility \(\gamma_K(x)\leq1\), the condition \(U_g\leq1\) certifies membership and \(L_g>1\) certifies nonmembership. For polar membership \(y\in K^{\circ}\), equivalently \(\sigma_K(y)\leq1\), the condition \(U_s\leq1\) certifies membership and \(L_s>1\) certifies nonmembership. For antipolar membership \(y\in C'\), equivalently \(m_C(y)\geq1\), the condition \(L_m\geq1\) certifies membership and \(U_m<1\) certifies nonmembership. Using only the interval information, the respective inconclusive cases are \(L_g\leq1<U_g\), \(L_s\leq1<U_s\), and \(L_m<1\leq U_m\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rigorous interval certifies gauge or polar membership when its upper endpoint is at most one and antipolar membership when its lower endpoint is at least one. The inconclusive crossing condition includes equality on different endpoints for the two threshold directions.
